#3433. 10 Hacks Every Reddit User Should Know

If you're looking for discussions, recommendations, or advice online, it's hard to avoid Reddit. From mainstream sports to niche crafts, it does seem that there's some kind of Reddit community for everyone. (And if there's not one, you can make one yourself.) If you're using Reddit, here are 10 hacks you should know about to improve your experience on the site.

Reddit used to let everyone view your post and comment history, but in recent years, you can make your profile private. You can hide your posts, comments, and the subreddits you're a part of. If you want to do this, click your profile icon once you've logged in to Reddit, and go to Settings > Profile. Alternatively, you can follow the direct link to Reddit's profile settings page. Click the drop-down menu next to Content & Activity, and select Hide all. You should also turn off Online Status on the same page to stop people from seeing when you're using Reddit.

Old Reddit lets you use the site's classic design, and I prefer it to the more modern UI. Old Reddit looks dated, but it doesn't have infinite scrolling, distracting animations, and a bunch of features designed to increase the time you spend on the platform. It's no wonder that Reddit is making it harder to access this version of the site. As long as it's around, you should switch to Old Reddit for a cleaner reading experience. You can do that by going to Reddit Settings > Preferences and enabling Default to Old Reddit. You can also visit old.reddit.com, though you'll need to sign in for access

Many subreddits use custom themes that range from beautiful to borderline unusable. If you want a more consistent UI across the site, you should disable these custom subreddit styles. Go to Reddit Settings > Preferences and turn off Use community themes. If you're using Old Reddit, click the preferences button in the top-right corner, and under "display options," disable allow subreddits to show me custom themes.

A multireddit is a feed that shows posts from a customized group of subreddits. You can think of it as a way to break out of Reddit's algorithms, and create your own Reddit feed. I use multireddits to follow all sports-related subs I'm interested in. I even have one for gaming, and one for fountain pens. It's a great way to create interest-specific feeds, and if you make them private, no one else can see them. To create one, click the Create custom feed button in the left pane in new Reddit. In the Old Reddit design, click the Create button in the left pane. Be sure to select the Private button to keep it from showing up for others. You can add as many subreddits as you like to the list, and bookmark the feed to access it whenever you wish to.

Reddit has recently adopted an Instagram-like experience for its feeds. It removed the ability to sort posts by new, controversial, best, etc., and instead offers "For You" and "Following." If you dislike this change, you can bypass it. I use Reddit on mobile Safari, and I recommend an extension called Sink It for Reddit. It can automatically redirect you to Old Reddit, and there's a feature that optimizes it for mobile, which brings back the old sorting options. You can also use third-party apps such as RedReader for Android, or RDX for Reddit on an iPhone or iPad to restore the old sorting options for Reddit posts.

After all these years, Reddit's built-in search still leaves something to be desired—at least, on the surface. To find posts on Reddit faster, use search filters on the site. For instance, adding "title:" to your search will limit the results to post titles, and boolean operators such as AND, OR, and NOT also work for advanced searches on the site.

#3432. Michael Keaton and Son Sean Douglas Talk Grief, Directing, and Their First-Ever Film Collaboration

The short film presents a unique challenge for its creative team. Despite its compressed timeframe, the screenwriter still has to fit in the story they wish to tell, the director has to bring that vision to life and meld it with their own, and the actor has to make their character as fully realized as possible. When it's done wrong, a short's brief runtime still feels like an eternity. But when it's done right, it can be powerful, leaving the viewer wishing the film ran far longer. Sweetwater, a 21-minute exploration of grief, unresolved family relationships and AI, created by the father/son duo of screenwriter Sean Douglas and actor/director Michael Keaton, falls into the latter category. In a Collider exclusive, Douglas and Keaton share their thoughts on the timely, thought-provoking 2025 short.

Commissioned as part of Google's "AI on Screen" initiative, Sweetwater opens on Robert Rogers (Keaton) making his way to his childhood home, the titular Sweetwater, the estate of his recently-deceased mother, celebrity singer/performer Bettie Rogers (Kyra Sedgwick). As he begins preparing Sweetwater for sale, he comes across a device sent by a long-time fan of Bettie's. The device projects an AI-generated, holographic recreation of Bettie, whose knowledge of the home and her life is detailed and thorough.

"Thorough," that is, to a degree. Hologram Bettie knows the facts culled from public data and internet archives, but has no knowledge of the intimate details of her real life, or the personal moments spent with Robert as he was growing up. Seeing his mother as she was feels like a shock to the grieving Robert, who initially tries to keep his distance from the holographic double. AI Bettie has no idea why, of course, and carries on engaging with Robert in the folksy, charming manner that marked her public persona.

It doesn't take long for Robert to engage, wanting to believe the hologram is genuinely his mother, wanting to ask about the decisions she made that affected his life — before coming back to the harsh realization that whatever unresolved history there is between them can't be turned around by this Bettie. Yet that line becomes less distinct as the movie progresses, coming to a conclusion that seems to erase it altogether.

Brilliant sci-fi visions that ruin everyday objects.

Sweetwater is a movie of big ideas — one that leaves it up to the viewer to answer for themselves. Has AI helped Robert through his grief, bringing him healing? Or has it, for all intents and purposes, kept his mother "alive," thus preventing that healing from happening at all? It's sharply written, and Keaton the director has a deft touch with his framing, keeping a clear separation between Bettie and Robert at the start that gradually lessens as the film progresses (interestingly, "Bettie" becomes less glitchy, too, an artistic decision that suggests she may be evolving).

Keaton the actor uses his innate ability to express the inner emotions that the words can't, while Sedgwick paces her performance wonderfully, beginning as a replica of Bettie that knows the facts before transforming into something deeper. That it does all this within a 21-minute runtime is a testament to how all the pieces came together to create a strong, effective, and good short film.

Collider was given the opportunity to conduct a written interview with both Sean Douglas and Michael Keaton about Sweetwater.

Sean Douglas is first and foremost a songwriter, known for his Grammy-nominated work with a massive variety of musical artists. What prompted him to write Sweetwater: an idea that wouldn't fit in a 3-minute song, or a story he sought to write as a screenplay from day one?

"As much as I love writing a concise pop song, after many years of that I found myself wanting to stretch out a little and write stories that can’t be contained in that form. Sweetwater is obviously a small story by film standards but it was really satisfying to make something that could take its time compared to a song. I have a music-centric feature that’s in development with some great talent attached and, while I’m still primarily a songwriter, it’s nice to balance that side with screenwriting."

For his part, Keaton added his input about what he found to be the most interesting aspect of the film, saying that of the two journeys in Sweetwater – Robert's pivot from fearing the AI to embracing it, and Bettie's transformation from knowing the facts alone to an almost-human reaction of recognition – the latter is the most fascinating. He then offered insight into what it was like to bring as complex a character as Robert to life in such a brief performance:

"Good for you for noticing, thank you! [It] was complex, lots to try to 'get done' as an actor in 2 (!) days while directing."

Sweetwater is about the son of a well-known celebrity, and as the son of one himself, one would think that much of Douglas' own experience is reflected in the film. Not so fast, he notes:

"You know, I’m slightly embarrassed to say I didn’t think about the celebrity parent parallel much while writing. I know that seems like a real lack of self-awareness. The personal element that was most front of mind was the theme of personal loss. My mother passed away sixteen years ago, and people who’ve gone through that would agree the cognitive dissonance of someone being there one day and gone the next is kind of mind-bending and leaves you open to, or desperate for some way to commune with that person.

I’ve also always been fascinated with the idea of Graceland-type places that are both a family home with personal memories and a place to be shared with the adoring public, much like the celebrity parent. So clearly the celebrity parent thing was present the whole time, and I’m more transparent and less mysterious than I’d like to believe!"

Keaton was then asked to reflect on his role as the director — a title he took on in 2008's The Merry Gentlemen, and then not again until 2023 with Knox Goes Away, before picking it up again with this film and the upcoming Road to Ruin. He was delightfully candid about what drove him into directing:

"I always wanted to, and always considered myself a kind of storyteller, [which is] an actor's job, really. No one would push for me back then, because it wouldn’t make anyone money. Also, I was lazy about it, probably. Also, as an actor, I can’t stand waiting around in a trailer most of the day."

Finally, Sweetwater opened at the inaugural Leander Film Festival in Leander, Texas, where it screened on Saturday, November 14th in Film Alley (fun fact: Renée Zellweger’s directorial debut, They, was also screened). Douglas was asked about the festival, and about future release plans:

"I’m really honored that the folks from Leander Film Festival reached out about featuring the film. It’s exciting to get it in front of an audience of film fans actively seeking out something new. Release plans are still being sorted out, but for now I’m just glad it’s getting eyeballs at festivals like Leander."

So keep an eye out for Sweetwater. You'll be glad you did.

#3431. 10 Hacks Every Hulu User Should Know

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

If you don't like the content Hulu is suggesting for you, you have several options to curate your recommendations. "Disliking" a show or movie removes it from your Home view and You May Also Like entirely, so the only way you'll see that content is if you search for it. You can dislike on the Details page if you're watching on your TV or use the thumbs down on mobile or web. (The "Like" button will obviously influence your algorithm in the opposite way). If your "Continue Watching" queue is cluttered with shows you started but didn't like enough to finish, you can remove them from your watch history as well as the My Stuff list. This, too, will allow content to remain searchable but not suggested in other areas of the app.

If PIN protection is enabled, users must enter a four-digit PIN when switching between profiles on a single account. This is intended as a parental control feature, since it's available on non-Kids profiles and can keep children from accessing more mature content on an adult's profile. However, you can also enable this feature to keep other users from seeing your viewing history and preferences or influencing your algorithm by watching their content under your profile (accidentally or on purpose). To set up a PIN, log into your account on Hulu's website, select your profile, and go to Manage Profiles > Parental Controls. You'll have to choose a PIN and enter your password to confirm the changes.

Another approach to protecting your profile and algorithm is to set up separate profiles for specific use cases, such as when you have guests or if you host watch parties for certain shows. This keeps content from influencing your recommendations and prevents other viewers from seeing what's in your watch history or saved content (especially if there are things you want to keep private).

If you find that subtitles and captions are too bold—or not visible enough—you can change the font, color, size, and style from the default so they enhance your viewing experience rather than detracting from it. Hulu allows you to adjust the color and opacity of the font, background, and window so you get the right contrast, and you can also select the specific font and font scaling. On your streaming device, go to Settings > Subtitles & Captions, then hit the back button on your remote to save your preferences. You can update these settings on mobile and desktop as well.

If you have a long list of shows and films to watch but can't decide what to start next, look for the "Expiring Soon" badge to see which titles are leaving the service in the next two weeks. Badges display the number of days remaining, so you can determine what to prioritize and whether it's worth diving in based on how much time you have to finish before the expiration date. Go to "My Stuff" to monitor saved titles that are expiring soon.

If you've been watching Hulu under an account shared with family or friends and need to switch to your own subscription, you can transfer your profile to keep your watch history and settings intact instead of starting from scratch. You can initiate a profile transfer on a TV-connected device. Note that account holders have to approve transfer requests within seven days, and once expired, transfer requests cannot be resubmitted—so be sure to let the primary user know that you've made the request.

If you've shared your Hulu login information with friends or activated your account on devices you don't own, you may want to regularly audit where your account is being used and remove any that don't need access. This includes TVs in Airbnbs and hotels. If you stay logged in, unauthorized users may have access to your Hulu account and personal data. You can see activated devices (and their activation date) under Your Account > Watch Hulu on Your Devices > Manage Devices. Click Remove next to old or unrecognized devices.

Hulu has an offline mode that allows you to download shows and movies to watch when you don't have a network connection. This is useful for traveling or when you know your wifi or cell service will be limited. Downloads are only available on supported iOS and Android devices, which means you may have to consider how much space your content takes up. You can select High for video quality if you want maximum resolution, but you may want to choose Standard if you are short on storage. This option is available under Downloads > Settings > Video Quality on iOS and Account > Settings > Downloads > Video Quality on Android. Note that once you click play on downloaded content, you have 48 hours to watch it before it expires—so don't start it unless you are ready.

If you have a Hulu + Live TV subscription, you must designate a "Home" network, which determines the local channels included in your plan. You can update your location up to four times within a 12-month period, but this limitation is meant to prevent viewers outside a household from sharing a subscription. Hulu does allow you to stream live TV on mobile when you're away from your home network (within the U.S.) as long as you access your account on that network every 30 days. If you travel often, check in with your mobile device frequently to avoid being locked out when you're away. Note that you can still watch streaming content with no restrictions.

#3430. 'Calvin and Hobbes' Best Miss Wormwood Quote Is Still Among the Smartest in Comic Strip History

You do need an education, this is not thought control

Bill Watterson walked a few different tightropes when he created Calvin and Hobbes, one of which involved Calvin's relationship with school. It would've been easy to make it simply antagonistic, with Calvin as the hero fighting back against the dark forces of educational conformity, a bit like a comic adaptation of Pink Floyd's "Another Brick in the Wall." Any number of later webcomics that were unsubtly inspired by Calvin and Hobbes went this way, at least at first.

Instead, Watterson was always careful to clarify that the biggest problem with Calvin's education is Calvin himself. His general attitude is likely familiar to anyone who spent any time as the "smart kid" in a public school: he knows everything there is to know about the things he likes and doesn't care enough to fake his way through anything else. If he was being graded on paleontology, comic books, or abstract snowman art, Calvin would be a straight-A student. Instead, he's struggling through basic math and early American history.

That leaves his teacher, Miss Wormwood, in an unfortunate position. In the few glimpses we get of the other students in Calvin's class, like Susie Derkins, Miss Wormwood doesn't have too many problem kids. It's just Moe, the class bully, who might not even be in Miss Wormwood's class, and Calvin, who's a force of pure chaos.

Like most of the rest of the Calvin and Hobbes supporting cast, we deliberately don't know that much about Miss Wormwood. Like Calvin's parents, she doesn't have a first name. The few details that Watterson provided include that she's only five years from retirement, she smokes like a chimney, and every once in a while, Calvin drives her to the point where she guzzles antacid straight out of the bottle. She's a near-universal stand-in for a particular sort of elderly American public school teacher, who've reached the end of their careers and are just marking time until they're pensioned off.

Watterson has noted several times, such as on his old official website, that Miss Wormwood's unusual name is a reference to the apprentice demon in C.S. Lewis' 1942 Christian novel The Screwtape Letters. The literary Wormwood is an understudy to Screwtape, both of whom are in the business of tempting humans into sin.

Despite her nominative origins, Miss Wormwood isn't really an antagonist in Calvin and Hobbes. (School as an institution is, to some extent, but she isn't.) She's simply someone that, in Watterson's words, really believes in the power of education. It's just too bad that the people she's trying to educate don't really appreciate it.

In most of the best comics that feature Miss Wormwood, she's an almost incidental presence. For example, she makes a silent appearance in one of the best Spaceman Spiff strips, shaking Calvin out of a particularly vivid daydream.

To be fair, this is the case for almost every character in Calvin and Hobbes who isn't Calvin or Hobbes. Calvin's parents both occasionally get a strip or two in the spotlight, but the focus is otherwise squarely on Calvin.

That being said, if you had to point to a single best strip for Miss Wormwood, there's really only one contender in my mind. It's a simple strip from 1992, which is part of a larger running gag about Calvin constantly challenging school as an institution.

"What assurance do I have that this education is adequately preparing me for the 21st century?" Calvin demands during class. "Am I getting the skills I'll need to effectively compete in a tough, global economy? I want a high-paying job when I get out of here! I want opportunity!"

Miss Wormwood's reaction is to get right in his face, in a bit of angry-teacher body language I remember from when I was a kid. "In that case, young man, I suggest you start working harder," she tells Calvin. "What you get out of school depends on what you put into it."

It's the one time Miss Wormwood manages something that could be seen as a victory, as usually Calvin is the one to drive her crazy. This time, she gets the last word, as well as offering a useful piece of advice to any struggling student.

#3428. How to Make Sure an 'Onion' Site on the Dark Web Is Legitimate

Thankfully, Tor Browser already has a cryptography-backed feature that can verify the authenticity of an onion site, by confirming whether it has end-to-end encryption and extended validation certificates. Here's how this feature works, where it falters, as well as what other red flags you should look for.

While phishing on the dark web works as it does on the clear web, scammers have a few unique advantages due to the secretive nature of the environment. Most importantly, you can’t just glance at an onion link to tell if the site is genuine. Normal website URLs tend to be short and memorable, while onion links are 56-character strings of alphanumeric text that look mostly like gibberish.

When you try to connect, Tor Browser verifies the URL against the originating website’s cryptographic key, which is how you know nobody has hijacked the address or tampered with it midway. But since this has the unwanted effect of making domains harder to recall, scammers have a much easier time generating lookalike addresses or creating website clones.

For example, many popular websites use “vanity prefixes” to make their onion addresses more easily identifiable or to add some branding appeal. That means their 56-character onion link starts with something like “facebook,” “bbcnews,” or “ciadotgov.” But scammers can use a free tool like mkp224o to generate lookalike addresses with the same vanity prefix as the legitimate website, which gives users a false sense of security.

Of course, most dark web users don’t type addresses directly into Tor Browser; they use dark web directories like the Hidden Wiki to find useful onion sites relevant to their search. Scammers will create fake search engines or link directories to point users to their fake websites, like when the Ahmia search engine discovered that a copy of its platform was directing users to 255 cloned services back in 2015.

Of course, it’s possible to orchestrate phishing attempts that don’t involve cloning sites at all. Researchers at Freie Universität Berlin describe a sophisticated technique where attackers serve the real website through their own reverse proxy, which lets them manipulate parts of the site or log your online activity without your awareness. In 2019, ESET even found a trojanized version of Tor Browser that replaced Bitcoin addresses on websites to direct payments to hackers. So both genuine websites and your browser itself are also vulnerable to manipulation if you download or access them from an unverified source.

There are a few best practices to avoid phishing attacks when using the dark web. None of them are foolproof on their own, but together, they considerably lower the risk of ending up on a fake or manipulated website.

On the desktop version of Tor Browser, you can access an onion site using a shortened version of its URL called an Onion Name. For now, this feature only works with SecureDrop, so newsrooms can establish tip lines with addresses like mysitename.securedrop.tor.onion, which would then redirect to the 56-character original onion address. This feature is in active development, so more platforms might support it in the future.

When you load up an onion site using the Tor Browser, you’ll see an onion icon on the address bar, which confirms that your connection is end-to-end encrypted. But you can also click on the onion icon to check if the site has an Extended Validation (EV) certificate, which tells you that its authenticity has been verified by a trusted certificate authority like DigiCert. While not every legitimate onion site will have an EV certificate, famous ones like Facebook tend to.

On the other hand, if you see a caution sign next to the onion icon, that means the site is using a self-signed or expired certificate that isn’t guaranteed by a trusted authority. It may also imply that the site is being served over an insecure URL. This doesn’t definitely tell you it’s a phishing site, but it’s a red flag to watch out for nevertheless.

Don’t rely on search engines, link directories, Reddit threads, or Telegram channels too heavily on the dark web. Once you’re sure you’ve found the onion address for a genuine site, bookmark it so you can access it directly the next time you want to visit.

If you realized that you’ve been the victim of a phishing attempt, the first step is to close the browser window with the fake site and access the real onion address to reset any account passwords you may have accidentally divulged.

Also, generally try to enable two-factor authentication and PGP logins on any dark web account that supports it for added security. And if you downloaded Tor Browser from anywhere other than the official Tor Project site, uninstall it now and grab a fresh copy from the official address.

#3427. What Happens If We Break Letterboxd?

Earlier this month, the Trylon in Minneapolis gave audiences six chances over three days to see “Kanał,” Andrzej Wajda’s 1957 film about Polish resistance fighters retreating into the sewers of Warsaw. After opening night, programmer John Moret saw enthusiastic reviews on Letterboxd.

The next evening, he says, ticket sales picked up.

Moret could imagine the calculation for somebody still on the fence: “Oh, these people I trust went to go see this movie, and they loved it. And it’s just playing for two more days.”

On November 5, the New York Times reported that its parent company was in exclusive talks to buy Letterboxd for roughly $330 million. Under the deal being discussed, the popular film-logging site would likely keep operating on its own but use the Times Company’s advertising technology. Related Stories How GKIDS Home Releases Are Creating the Fandom They Want to See in the World IDA Documentary Awards 2026 Nominations: ‘You Can See Everything,’ ‘Concrete Land,’ and More Earn Nods

For theaters like the Trylon, what matters is whether cinephiles who went on opening night can still reach those who might go tomorrow. In 2026, that handoff is working remarkably well on Letterboxd.

Five days before “Kanał” opened, Ken Russell’s “The Devils” sold out at the Trylon on election night. Moret also co-founded the national Programmers’ Jam with Bret Berg, theatrical sales director at the American Genre Film Archive, and Dan Halsted of Portland’s Hollywood Theatre. When the Jam met in Los Angeles in May, Berg told IndieWire that programmers had access to more restorations than ever before; plus, more places to show them and a new audience coming through the doors.

We helped declare it the Golden Age of Repertory programming this spring. And when we spoke with Berg again this month, he said Letterboxd still drives “the FOMO of needing to be conversant in a movie of the moment.” For at least a few days in Minneapolis, that movie was “Kanał.”

Berg can see why a press company might be a good home for Letterboxd. He also remembers what the last sale made plain to him: Something cinephiles had spent years building was ultimately “just an asset to be bought and sold.” In the r/Letterboxd thread about the talks, one commenter saw an upside to a newspaper owning a site that rates movies. They also worried about paywalled features and ads, but liked the prospect of a ratings system free of “studios putting their fingers on the scale.”

If you come home from seeing a rep movie and write what you thought about it, your friends get a recommendation, the theater gets a little local press, Letterboxd itself gets something to put an ad next to, and as a matter of historical record? Years later, a “Kanał” fan who’s never even been to Minneapolis can land on the same page and read what it was like to see it with your crowd.

That’s a powerful engine for word-of-mouth, particularly among the very online. Moret keeps his own movie diary in a paper notebook these days, and told us he actually stopped posting what he watched on Letterboxd for a while because Trylon customers kept asking if that meant he was going to program it. “Sometimes a guy just wants to watch a movie,” he said.

Moret still regularly checks Letterboxd after screenings and uses that data to help shape his local scene. “I can see that night exactly how they responded,” he said. Moret said he’s seen Trylon patrons meet theater volunteers and follow them on Letterboxd afterward. He’s also heard from people who knew one another by their Letterboxd handles before they started going to showings together. Their community has real taste, and Moret’s job is to help subtly steer that momentum in exciting artistic directions.

He did have an ulterior motive for December’s Dede Allen series.

Moret explained to IndieWire that he wanted to show “Mike’s Murder,” James Bridges’ 1984 mystery starring Debra Winger as a bank teller trying to find out who killed her tennis instructor, and realized a Letterboxd user could make a pretty good list out of movies you didn’t know shared an editor like Allen. So, he put multiple of the craftsman’s offerings on the calendar — effectively allowing Trylon visitors to use a popular classic like “Dog Day Afternoon” on December 11 as an avenue toward “Mike’s Murder” on December 18. (Of course, both play in 35mm.)

On the supply end at the American Genre Film Archive, Berg reads the reviews from one town with the next town in mind. A joke review with thousands of likes might tell him very little about who’d pay to see a movie. But five people leaving a one-off screening at a DIY microcinema and feeling compelled to write about it could tell him quite a lot.

For someone deciding which films in the archive’s catalog deserve another look, that’s “some interesting free data,” and even Berg comes across movies he’s never heard of. Three and a half stars on Letterboxd is enough to make him give one a closer look. Then, he wants to know what kind of time people had. “How many audience moments are there? That’s what I care about.”

For a horror movie, he might be counting jump scares. With Herzog, he’s thinking about how many iconic images there are. (Referencing Les Blank’s “Ship of Dreams,” I personally suggested that the nation craves the sight of a steamship being pushed up a mountain. “Oh, it’s true,” Berg said.)

Berg also named Spectacle in Brooklyn and Whammy! in Los Angeles as places where he could count on hearing from a few people whether a movie made an impression. He said he can look for the same things he would on any research viewing, but with the added benefit of a crowd that makes a significant difference. Was everybody there to see a new restoration? How full was the room exactly?

Berg could always pick up the phone and ask someone like Moret how a screening went in Minneapolis. But Letterboxd gives them both a way to see and respond to the same information, connecting what happens in one theater to what programmers are noticing hit elsewhere.

Berg also thinks about who’s had the chance to write film books previously, and who has been taken seriously as a critic on a national stage. He singled out trans critics among the writers who can find an audience on Letterboxd without first persuading an editor to commission a review. In the end, the person who finally gets you to watch a movie might write three sentences half a century after the original reviews ran. They might also be the only person you encounter who’s heard of it.

If the people writing those Letterboxd reviews scatter across half a dozen sites, Berg could still go looking for them but it would take longer. And if Letterboxd imploded altogether, he’d expect “a return to gut feeling” that wouldn’t be bad — but might give the audience less of a voice.

Berg has some experience with the decision to leave. He still uses Vimeo for his day job, but the price helped persuade him to move his own project, Museum of Home Video, to a cheaper service. Finding another place to stream was manageable, and the Letterboxd equivalent of that transition is doable for most users too. First, it would mean finding another place to put your film log and reviews. Then, you’d have to find the people whose retro picks and ideas got you to sign up in the first place.

In that same Letterboxd Reddit thread, one person was already looking for the exit. “Any other apps people know about with similar list-building functionality?” they asked.

Andrew Masyk, the founder of rival tracking site Simkl, says its importer can bring over your watchlist, ratings, and the full text of your reviews, and custom lists can come over using a separate tool. That said, the comments and follows stay behind. “People have to find each other again, and that’s the hardest part of moving,” he wrote.

Masyk has every business reason to make switching easy. Even so, he figures people who have spent years keeping a movie diary on Letterboxd are mostly inclined to stay put. “What moves people is the product changing under them: core features going behind a paywall, heavier ads, or getting your data out becoming harder.” His test for a buyer is whether they keep that exit open. “The export button matters more than who owns the company,” he wrote.

Yes, the export button can save a Letterboxd review but the friend who used to see it in their feed still has to find it — and that can get more difficult long before anyone actually leaves Letterboxd. If a buyer gave sponsored posts more room in the feed, for instance, you could still log every film you see while missing the three sentences from a friend that would’ve gotten you to your local theater in time.

If Letterboxd breaks, the Trylon loses one way to fill a seat, and a programmer in another town loses one way to tell whether “Kanał” might fill a few seats there, too. As for regular film fans? Hear about “Kanał” on Monday, and you can go. Hear about it on Wednesday, and you’ve missed the boat.

#3425. 5 Great LitRPG Novels That Are Nothing Like ‘Dungeon Crawler Carl’

The LitRPG genre (short for literary role-playing game) has taken off like a rocket over the last few years. LitRPG has been around for decades, but the emergence of Matt Dinniman's bestselling Dungeon Crawler Carl series has seen it move from an underground niche to a genre with dedicated shelves at chain book stores. Dungeon Crawler Carl has the zeitgeist in a way we haven't seen in some time, and it is paving the way for countless others. We're already seeing other hits like He Who Fights With Monsters appear in places like Target and Walmart, signaling the LitRPG genre is continuing to expand its footprint.

One common misconception, however, is that Dungeon Crawler Carl is totally representative of the wider LitRPG genre. While the entire series is fantastic, it's a small slice of what is a surprisingly large genre pie. There are so many hidden gems within progression sci-fi and fantasy, and Dungeon Crawler Carl is just the tip of the iceberg.

So if you enjoyed your time in the dungeon with Carl and Donut, but you're looking to see what else LitRPG has to offer, here's a list of five awesome stories in the genre that are guaranteed to take you in completely different directions.

Matt Dinniman has often described Dungeon Crawler Carl as a horror story, and it's not difficult to understand why. The bigger universe epic happening throughout the series is haunting at times, and there are plenty of body horror motifs stuffed into the dungeon itself. That said, Dungeon Crawler Carl doesn't necessarily fit into the traditional horror genre box, but fans wanting old-school scares and classic horror archetypes do have another series they can turn to.

Rob M. Lastrel's The Game at Carousel series is a horror movie molded into LitRPG form. The first book, The Bystander, sees a group of friends arrive in the small town of Carousel, only to be brought into a survival game in which they all take on the tropes of horror movie characters. Those archetypes, including the Film Buff and Final Girl, evolve as the friends play into their roles, and they have to figure out how to use those tropes to survive an onslaught of killers.

This isn't the first time Tree of Aeons has come up here, and it probably won't be the last. That's because the concept of this book feels deliriously unhinged, but spaizzzer turns it into one of the most thoughtful and compelling narratives within the LitRPG genre.

The eight-book series follows a protagonist that is reborn into a vast world of magic and fantasy. Instead of becoming a great warrior or skilled sorcerer, however, Matt is reborn into this world as a tree. That's right, the main character is literally a tree, and the story couldn't be more enjoyable. As a tree, Matt finds himself amidst an ongoing war with demons, and he must figure out how to level up his seemingly limited abilities to help the warriors around him.

It lacks the bombastic energy of a series like Dungeon Crawler Carl, but Tree of Aeons replaces it with introspection and ingenuity. Not only is this series unlike Dungeon Crawler Carl, it's unlike pretty much anything you've ever read.

While it does share the similar comedic trappings of Dungeon Crawler Carl, A.P. Scribe's hit series is an adventure of a completely different scale. Instead of saving the entire human race by working through increasingly deadly levels of a galactic reality TV show, Dungeons & Deliveries is about a regular guy just trying to deliver pizzas on time.

In a fantastical version of Toronto, protagonist Alex is struggling to get by. Unable to get hired by any guilds or adventuring parties, he takes on a job delivering pizzas. Unfortunately for him, many of his clients turn out to be dungeon bosses, and he has to dive deep into their dungeons to get them their pies, trying hard just to make it back to work in one piece.

Hopping through worlds with a New York plumber makes for a fun and familiar adventure.

There are slice-of-life progression fantasy stories, which take away the massive stakes of books like Dungeon Crawler Carl and focus on the more everyday lives of characters instead. Then there's Heretical Fishing, which goes so much further than many of those other titles, creating what might be the heaviest "vibes only" saga in all of LitRPG.

It may not be for everyone, but reading Jobson's Heretical Fishing series often feels like sitting out on the peer and listening to the soft sounds of the water as a cool breeze blows against your face. It's as relaxing an experience as you'll find in LitRPG, and it stands out amongst the crowd for all the ways it forces both its characters and you to slow down a little bit.

If you want something truly out of left field, and not about a sentient tree, then you may want to turn to Cassius and Tang's Mimic and Me series. This hilarious and heartfelt saga is about a protagonist who is left on death's door at the very beginning of the series, and only remains alive when a seemingly monstrous mimic stumbles across him. The mimic ends up bonding with the character and, from there, it turns into a Venom-esque buddy trip through a LitRPG world.

The story is nothing like Dungeon Crawler Carl, but fans of the famous DCC audiobooks will be keen to check out those versions of Mimic and Me, as Jeff Hayes is a featured voice in the productions. Ryan H. Reid is the main narrator for the audiobooks and Dorrie Sacks is featured alongside Hayes.

#3424. How Long Does It Take To Beat GTA 6?

If you couldn't guess by its 210 GB file size, Grand Theft Auto 6 is gigantic. Rockstar's latest open-world game is stuffed to the brim with things to do and steal. It also sports the beefiest story of any GTA game to date. Jason and Lucia star in a sprawling crime epic that takes the couple all around the state of Leonida. While it's difficult to put a consistent hour count on a true 100% playthrough of GTA 6, we do know that you won't be able to binge it all in one long weekend.

Here's how long it takes to beat GTA 6's story depending on how much side-content you intend to complete.

Even if we're just talking about how long it will take you to beat the story and reach the end credits, expect to spend a lot of time with GTA 6. In our fastest playthrough, we were able to complete the game in around 53 hours. While that playthrough was focused on clearing the story, it still included a healthy number of side-quests, optional robberies, mini-golf games, and plenty of free-form exploration.

A faster playthrough may be possible, but note that GTA 6 features several points where players will either have to amass a certain amount of money or wait for a call to proceed to the next story mission. Even if you only plan on playing for the story, you'll likely still need to do some side-activities to get through it all with enough money to reach the final missions.

Players who want to take their time can expect an even longer experience. In another playthrough that was more focused on completing lots of optional side-activities, our save file crossed the 100-hour mark. That matches what Rockstar North co-studio head Rob Nelson recently told Polygon about his most recent full-story playthrough before launch, which he said took him just over 100 hours, in a run that he described as "rushed."

Though that’s a wide range of hours, what we’ve seen so far in testing lines up with How Long To Beat's data on Red Dead Redemption 2. User playtime data puts an average main story playthrough at around 52 hours and one with a focus on side-content at 89 hours, which matches with what we found in GTA 6.

All in all, expect to spend 70 to 80 hours clearing the main story unless you plan to mainline it. That makes GTA 6 the series' longest game by a wide margin, so budget your time accordingly.

One of Jean-Luc Picard's most intense and popular story arcs is none other than the iconic Locutus of Borg storyline, which remains one of the most unforgettable moments in Star Trek history. First introduced in The Next Generation's legendary two-part episode "The Best of Both Worlds," Locutus was a terrifying turning point for Picard, who was captured and assimilated by the Borg Collective and then turned into a full-on baddie.

While Picard was eventually rescued and restored to his former self, his experience with the Borg would haunt him for decades, becoming a defining part of his character's legacy. Locutus has since become one of Star Trek's most notorious villains, despite technically being a twisted version of one of its greatest heroes.

Now, more than 35 years after his original debut, Locutus of Borg is officially making another return, bringing Picard's dark chapter back into the spotlight in an exciting new way.

Locutus of Borg is officially back in Magic: The Gathering as part of the massive Star Trek crossover, which launched on November 13, 2026. The iconic villain appears in We Are the Borg, one of four new Commander decks released alongside the larger set, bringing together some of the franchise's most recognizable characters and storylines.

The white, blue, and black Commander deck is led by the Borg Queen, with Locutus serving as an alternative commander. The entire deck revolves around assimilating enemy creatures, building an unstoppable army of Borg, and overwhelming opponents through sheer numbers.

"Locutus of Borg" is a legendary 3/3 artifact creature with lifelink, costing four mana to summon and one that comes with a borderless version as well. His most interesting ability allows every artifact creature under your control to create a 1/1 Borg artifact creature token whenever it deals combat damage to an opposing player.

It's a great interpretation of Picard's villainous alter ego, reflecting the Borg's ability to continuously expand the Collective by assimilating other beings. Essentially, the more Borg you have who land an attack, the more powerful your army becomes. The Borg Queen complements Locutus perfectly, giving artifact creatures +2/+2 while using the new Assimilate mechanic to bring enemy creatures under your control.

There's even a second version of Locutus in the larger MTG release included as part of the Showdown at Sector 001 scene card set, called "Locutus, the One Who Speaks," which gives artifact creatures +1/+1 and can be discarded to damage an enemy creature while restoring life (see above).

The deck also features several recognizable pieces of Borg tech, including the Class-4 Tactical Cube, Borg Scout Sphere, and Queen's Diamond. There's even a special "The Best of Both Worlds" Saga card and "Battle of Wolf 359," both directly referencing Picard's original transformation.

For longtime Star Trek fans, it's an exciting addition to the crossover, bringing one of the franchise's best villains back while allowing players to experience the Borg Collective's relentlessness firsthand.

#3422. Tilda Swinton, Mark Ruffalo, Jacques Audiard, and Others Join in Protest of Jafar Panahi’s Prison Sentence

The film community is marshaling to support Oscar-nominated, dissident Iranian filmmaker Jafar Panahi, who was given a prison sentence of five years and one month by the Tehran Revolutionary Court back in October.

A letter initiated by the International Coalition for Filmmakers at Risk (and shared with Variety) so far features more than 200 signatories “deeply concerned by reports of the new prison sentence of five years and one month issued by the Tehran Revolutionary Court against Iranian filmmaker Jafar Panahi, in absentia.” Panahi returned to Iran in the spring following the end of Neon’s awards run for his Cannes Film Festival Palme d’Or winner “It Was Just an Accident,” nominated for Best International Feature and Best Original Screenplay at the 2026 Academy Awards. Related Stories What Happens If We Break Letterboxd? How GKIDS Home Releases Are Creating the Fandom They Want to See in the World

Actors and filmmakers who’ve signed the letter include Mark Ruffalo, Tilda Swinton, Jacques Audiard, Kleber Mendonça Filho, Catherine Breillat, Bertrand Bonello, Alice Braga, Arthur Harari, Asif Kapadia, Lucrecia Martel, Rob Epstein, Rodrigo Teixeira, Apichatpong Weerasethakul, Geeta Gandbhir, and many more. Festival leaders who signed the letter include Berlinale director Tricia Tuttle, New York Film Festival artistic director Dennis Lim, Venice’s Alberto Barbera, Telluride head Julie Huntsinger, and others — many of whom have hosted Panahi’s films across the last four decades.

Previously, Panahi was sentenced to one year in prison and a two-year ban on leaving Iran in December, in absentia. The new October 2026 sentence carries additional penalties, as the letter notes, including confiscation of his assets, freezing of his bank accounts, a two-year travel ban, and a two-year social media ban.

Panahi has a long history of legal entanglements with the Iranian government, which his films have criticized, including numerous imprisonments, a temporary house arrest, and being barred from participating in filmmaking activities. These punitive actions have frequently forced Panahi to make his films in secret or structure them around his filmmaking process or legal status — such as in the 2022 Venice prize winner “No Bears.”

Panahi’s bank accounts were frozen around the October sentencing, according to Panahi’s attorney Mostafa Nili. Panahi could not be reached in October for the sentencing, according to reports, despite being present in Iran as recently as September.

“In March 2026, the 66-year-old Mr. Panahi courageously decided to return to Iran, aware of the risks but having always spoken of his deep love for his country, and for his desire to stay and work there. In October 2026 he learned of the new court verdict against him after his bank accounts were frozen, his lawyer, Mostafa Nili, said in a statement to the Iranian press. The new charges against him remain unclear, but appear consistent with repeated efforts to intimidate him into ceasing his filmmaking. The case will now go to regional court, and the sentence can be appealed. This requires resources, but all of Mr. Panahi’s accounts have been blocked,” the letter states.

“We stand in solidarity with Mr. Panahi and all Iranians facing persecution for their work at the hands of their own government. We call on the Tehran Revolutionary Court to rescind all actions to penalize and imprison Mr. Panahi and to abide by the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights to which the Iranian government is a signatory.”

See the letter in full here. The Cannes Film Festival issued a similar letter in protest earlier this week.

#3420. ‘Gentle Monster’ Review: Léa Seydoux Learns the Truth About Her Husband in Marie Kreutzer’s Tough Study of Child Sex Abuse

[Editor’s note: This review was originally published on May 15, 2026 during the 2026 Cannes Film Festival. Netflix will release the film on its streaming platform on Wednesday, November 18.]

Marie Kreutzer’s “Gentle Monster” opens with virtuoso musician Lucy Weiss (Léa Seydoux) sitting at the piano in her Munich apartment and plunking out a stilted but affecting cover of Charles & Eddie’s neo-soul classic “Would I Lie to You?”

This is before her Austrian husband Philip (Laurence Rupp) — a documentary TV producer of marginal success — comes home in a burnout panic that spurs them to permanently relocate their family to a cottage in the German countryside. Before the authorities bang on their door with a warrant for Philip’s arrest, forcing Lucy to ride the elevator up to the clearly designated “child porn” floor of the local police station in order to learn the facts of his case. Before she begins to wonder, in rage and terror and desperate layers of self-protective doubt, whether the father of her young son Johnny (Malo Blanchet) might actually be capable of preying on other kids, or even his own.  Related Stories Tilda Swinton, Mark Ruffalo, Jacques Audiard, and Others Join in Protest of Jafar Panahi’s Prison Sentence What Happens If We Break Letterboxd?

Among other things, this tough and unflinching social drama is a study in how painful it can be for a rhetorical question — like “Would I lie to you, baby?,” for example — to sour into the stomach-churning stuff of an urgent mystery. For the terms of a relationship to change faster than the facts of the matter are able to keep up with, let alone the feelings that might attend to them. “There is no ‘off button’ for pedophilia,” someone explains to Lucy at one point. There isn’t an “off button” for love either.

Perhaps that’s why Lucy was able to ignore the signs for so long, some of which the audience is given the chance to see in a dark and disquieting flashback that Kreutzer cleverly interjects during the movie’s second act. Perhaps, despite the less intimate nature of their relationship, that’s why Kreutzer herself was so inclined to believe the male lead of her previous film (“Corsage”) when he privately disputed the rumors that he was guilty of similar crimes. Actor Florian Teichtmeister ultimately pleaded guilty to possessing more than 76,000 child sexual abuse files, more than half of which showed children under the age of 14.

While Kreutzer surely laments that situation on several different levels, this is neither a penitent film nor a self-exculpatory one (its origins trace back to before the production of “Corsage,” when the director read a newspaper article about a pedophile ring in North Rhine-Westphalia). It’s safe to assume that most people will feel sick to their souls on Lucy’s behalf, but “Gentle Monster” — its title pointedly depriving us of Lucy’s natural doubt — doesn’t make any overt pleas for sympathy, just as it doesn’t render Philip as the kind of demon that anyone might see coming a mile away.

In the context of such a terrible crime, Kreutzer is naturally less concerned with right and wrong than she is with the way that even the most sordid type of abuse is able to disguise itself in domesticity. If victims are our friends and neighbors, then it stands to reason that perpetrators are too.

Hard-nosed and realistic as far as these things go, “Gentle Monster” only makes a few concessions to movie logic. The first and most obvious of those is that Lucy is a fantastically chic public figure of some renown, a Jacob Collier-like pianist known for deconstructing famous pop songs written by men — everything from George Michaels’ “Freedom” to The Cure’s “Boys Don’t Cry.” The latter bop proves especially instructional, as Lucy is fascinated by the fact that men are so much more honest about their emotions in music than they are in real life. Her mission is to take apart their words and question the meaning behind them, a semi-credible gimmick that Seydoux is able to sell on the strength of her confidence alone.

It’s true, of course, that men should never be trusted, but Lucy will soon find that her own feelings are just as liable to lead her astray. First, she convinces herself that relocating to the sticks might fix whatever’s going on with Philip — a choice that inspires her mom, played by an underwritten Catherine Deneuve, to crack that, “For a female artist, there’s only one thing worse than having children: moving to the countryside.” Then, once Philip is brought up on charges, Lucy does what she can to downplay the evidence of his deviancy. All fathers take videos of their sons, after all. Most of them don’t shoot on 8mm film or frame close-ups of their kids for the length of a portrait sitting, but Philip still imagines himself as an artist (which explains why he seems to be so cucked by his wife’s success), and he’s prone to saying things like “Faces say so much only after you’ve looked at them for some time.”

There are no histrionic scenes in which Lucy screams at people for doubting her husband’s innocence, and Seydoux’s implosive performance makes it seem as though — a little less with every passing detail she discovers — Lucy is only mad at herself for believing Philip’s rationalizations. He was doing it for a documentary. He only uploaded a video of Johnny to earn trust from the pedophile community. He was just acting as a fence for illicit content because he felt emasculated by his lack of income. Whatever he can say to convince this woman that it’s easier to blame herself for overreacting than it would be to contend with the true nature of his crimes. Nothing much really happens in this movie after Philip’s initial arrest, but the world viscerally shudders under Lucy’s feet every time one of her husband’s alibis falls apart.

Lucy’s image of Philip — the one she loves and clings to — is like a song that’s stuck in her head, and deconstructing that song turns out to be a challenge of a different sort. Her only potential ally in that process is special investigator Elsa Kühn (Jella Haase), who’s caught more pedophiles like Philip than she can count. As unmovable as Lucy is unmoored, the working-class Elsa is defined by the relative calm with which she navigates her own personal crisis: a senile father who keeps harassing his nurses.

The obviousness with which Kreutzer introduces Elsa into this story as a foil is offset by the uncertainty of the character’s purpose. On the one hand, Elsa could also be seen as collateral damage — as another casualty of a man whose inner life has betrayed the role he was meant to play in his family. On the other hand, Elsa’s permissive reaction to her father’s abuse introduces a less gendered hypocrisy into the mix, as the lack of sympathy she feels towards Lucy is undercut by her refusal to confront the rot in her own house.

In a film that refuses to “resolve” any of its drama, or to glibly suggest that there’s anything constructive we can do about any of this aside from staring it in the face, Elsa’s subplot is left to awkwardly jut out from the side of the central story, a semi-effective distraction from the fact that Lucy has little to do but wait for the other shoe to drop and worry if she can contain the social blowback. “Gentle Monster” doesn’t quite get that far, as Kreutzer limits the drama to a slow drip of despair, its queasy suspense rooted in the question of how sick the revelations about Philip will have to get before Lucy is finally able to see him for what he is — to hear the man behind the song, so to speak.

And so the ugliness of pedophilia itself, rather than the specifics of how Lucy comes to grips with it, assumes center stage as Kreutzer’s primary subject. Full of feeling but starved of an outlet for it, Lucy is gradually woven into the fabric of Judith Kaufmann’s widescreen framing, which invites natural beauty into this grimdark story at the same time as it makes its subject feel inescapable. The world assumes the texture of a gilded cage; life goes on, some of it as sparkling as her in-laws’ picturebook summer house in the Austrian Alps, but Lucy remains trapped in the discordant hell that surrounds her, and that no one else can seem to hear. If only she had always known how to listen so closely.

“Gentle Monster” premiered at the 2026 Cannes Film Festival.

#3418. The 8 Best-Performed Audiobooks of All Time, Ranked

The concept of audiobooks was born alongside Thomas Edison's phonograph in the late 19th century, but actual "Talking Books" as a commercial category appeared in the 1930s as a tool for visually impaired readers without knowledge of or access to Braille to experience literature. In the years since, the medium has evolved greatly alongside technology like cassette tapes and CDs. Now, in the digital era, audiobooks have become such an abundant and mainstream product that even people with no kind of visual impairment have come to choose them as their preferred method of reading.

But while several incredible audiobooks have been produced over the years, a special few can easily be counted among the best, most vividly performed in the medium's history. A truly great narrator feels like they have a genuinely profound connection to the material, delivering each line with appropriate emotional weight and making it easier to understand the subtext of the original book. If they portray each character's voice with a distinct characterization, pace their cadence well, and fit the book's genre well, any narrator can make their audiobook performance go down in history as legendary.

Some of its narrative elements haven't aged perfectly, but in no way does that detract from the fact that Harper Lee's To Kill a Mockingbird is one of the greatest and most foundational American books ever written about racial prejudice, systemic injustice, and human nature. It was the novel that earned Lee a Pulitzer Prize in 1961, and it has aged wonderfully as one of the most influential Southern Gothic novels of the entire 20th century. Who better to narrate such a quintessential piece of Southern American literature than legendary Texas native Sissy Spacek?

Through sheer vocal authenticity and dramatic restraint, Spacek makes this one of the best audiobooks of all time. For one, the actress effectively uses her Southern drawl and cadence to make the small-town Alabama setting feel all the more immersive, elevating Lee's beautiful prose to make it feel all the more melodic. She also perfectly captures the spirit and personality of every character, with the way she marks the contrast between child Scout and adult Scout standing out as a particularly memorable narrative choice.

Where many of the best-narrated audiobooks in history were one-person shows, the Lincoln in the Bardo audiobook stands out as perhaps the greatest audiobook ever narrated by an ensemble cast. Written by George Saunders, this 2017 experimental novel is narrated by a shifting crowd of 166 spirits who are often unaware that they are dead. It's full of wonderfully surreal magical realism, making it such a special book that Saunders, who usually recorded his audiobooks himself, decided that he needed a full cast in order to do the text justice.

Saunders' friend Nick Offerman and his wife, Megam Mullally, agreed to perform in the audiobook cast and recruit a bunch of other narrators, including celebrities like Don Cheadle and non-celebrities like Saunders' family and friends. With a gargantuan 166-person cast, Lincoln in the Bardo easily takes the cake as the audiobook with the biggest narrator ensemble in history, and the resulting product feels surprisingly even and creatively coherent. With such different voices appearing over the course of seven and a half hours, the book's rhythmic prose, hypnotic pacing, and sense of humor are all elevated.

The Lord of the Rings began with J. R. R. Tolkien's publisher's request that he write a sequel to the mega-successful children's fantasy book The Hobbit. What started as more of a simple follow-up gradually started transforming into something far bigger and more ambitious, until we finally got what many would confidently call the most important and influential fantasy novel of the 20th century. Indeed, though it was published in three volumes between 1954 and 1955, The Lord of the Rings is technically all one huge fantasy epic, easily one of the most ambitious high fantasy books of all time.

After his participation in Peter Jackson's Middle-earth film trilogy, it was Andy Serkis who narrated the second-ever unabridged audiobook edition of the novel, also published in three separate volumes. Clocking in at roughly 65 hours, his take on this towering achievement of fantasy storytelling brings a unique and unforgettable voice not only to Gollum, but to every other character that takes part in Frodo's journey. Serkis also fully commits to the many songs and poems that Tolkien sprinkled across the novel, adding further vocal variety to an audiobook that was already exquisitely varied.

British author Joe Abercrombie's The First Law series is one of the greatest pieces of grimdark fantasy of the 21st century, composed of two trilogies, three standalone novels, and two short story collections. The book that started it all was The Blade Itself, the first chapter in the trilogy that's also titled The First Law. While it's undoubtedly one of the most essential dark fantasy masterpieces of the last 20 years, it's usually agreed upon among fans that several of its sequels are even better. When it comes to audiobook versions, though, there's no beating the original.

English actor and stage performer Steven Pacey, known for his work in shows like Blake's 7 and MobLand, narrates the Blade Itself audiobook with precisely the kind of gritty realism and razor-sharp comedic timing that a masterpiece like this would need. It's a masterclass in voice control where Pacey switches between the dramatically distinct voice of each character with the utmost ease, as well as a masterclass in dry British wit that complements Abercrombie's dark sense of humor flawlessly. As the book moves quickly from brutal action to slow-burning political scheming to moments of pure dark comedy, Pacey matches the rhythm of such transitions perfectly.

There can be no conversation about the best-narrated audiobooks in history without talking about the best-narrated biographies and autobiographies. Readers may point to many different books when asked about what the best-narrated autobiography of all time is, but there's one title that's bound to come up more often than most: Born a Crime, the comedic autobiography of South African comedian, writer, and political commentator Trevor Noah.

The book is primarily focused on Noah's childhood in South Africa after he was born to an illegal interracial relationship during the apartheid era, and this audiobook version has long been regarded as the gold standard of non-fiction narrated by the author. As a natural polyglot, a seasoned stand-up comedian, and an expert speaker thanks to his experience as a television host, Noah narrates Born a Crime not only with the deepest emotional intimacy possible, but also with a level of cultural authenticity that feels essential to the book.

J. K. Rowling's Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (published in the United States as Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone) took a couple of years to become a true commercial juggernaut, kicking off the most financially successful fantasy book series of all time. As such, it was entirely unsurprising when Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows broke the record as the book with the most volumes sold within 24 hours of release, instantly cementing itself as one of the best books of the 2000s.

Audiobook editions were released simultaneously on the day of the book's publication, with the UK edition being narrated by Stephen Fry and the US edition being narrated by Jim Dale. While both Fry and Dale broke the record for the most distinct character voices recorded by an individual on an audiobook at the time (with a whopping 146), there's something special about Dale's performance that earned him the 2008 Grammy for the Best Spoken Word Album for Children. Theatrical, energetic, and full of emotionally cathartic moments, Dale's narration is an all-timer.

The LitRPG genre is a category of speculative fiction where the story explicitly incorporates mechanics and tropes from video games and tabletop RPGs into the narrative, and as far as LitRPG novels go, it doesn't get any better than Matt Dinniman's Dungeon Crawler Carl series. The series was initially self-published until it was acquired by Ace Books in 2024. The first of the bunch is 2020's Dungeon Crawler Carl, one of those sci-fi and fantasy books that are perfect from start to finish.

Dinniman's studio, Soundbooth Theater, produced an audiobook of Dungeon Crawler Carl in 2021, narrated by voice artist Jeff Hays. Widely cited as a rare case where the audiobook edition of a book practically eclipses the print version, the Dungeon Crawler Carl audiobook is anchored by Hays' jaw-dropping vocal range, at times making it feel like you're listening to a full cast rather than a single performer. Seamlessly paced and full of humor, Hays' narration is absolute perfection.

Andy Weir has only published four novels so far in his career, but they have already been enough for him to establish and cement himself as one of the leading hard sci-fi authors currently working. His latest work is Project Hail Mary, widely praised as his magnum opus and one of those books that are a masterclass in hard sci-fi writing. The winner of the 2022 Audie Award for Audiobook of the Year, Ray Porter's unabridged audiobook has come to be praised by many as the single best-performed audiobook of all time.

After listening to Porter's performance once, it's hard to imagine ever revisiting Project Hail Mary in any other way again. It's the definitive way to experience the story, not only because the medium couples perfectly with the novel's heavy focus on themes of communication. Porter captures both Grace and Rocky's voices faultlessly, and he manages to turn the many complex scientific elements into exposition that feels surprisingly conversational and humorous. Energetic, well-paced, emotional, and tonally varied, it's some of the greatest narration that any audiobook has ever delivered.

#3417. 10-Episode HBO Max Fantasy Series Delivers A Masterclass In Bending Genres

Even though the show takes its name from an iconic horror author, one HBO miniseries is notable for its deft ability to blend a wide array of genres in its complex, compelling story. The miniseries format can be both a blessing and a curse for TV creators. On the one hand, its inherently self-contained style can allow creators to tell a perfect standalone story without worrying about renewals, as evidenced by HBO’s post-apocalyptic drama Station Eleven.

A near-flawless adaptation of author Emily St. John Mandel’s 2014 novel of the same name, Station Eleven would likely have struggled if the show needed to consider a second season storyline that expanded beyond the book’s plot. Instead, like Patrick Stewart’s breakout hit I, Claudius, the miniseries was a success precisely because Station Eleven was a miniseries, so the show didn’t have to expand its plot beyond the novel’s already-cohesive story.

Of course, there are also challenges when it comes to adapting books into miniseries, especially when it is not clear what genre category the story slots into. Although Hulu’s dystopian series The Handmaid’s Tale] is often classified as a straightforward sci-fi story, the show also leans into the psychological horror of its premise. Similarly, the 2020 critical hit Lovecraft Country saw HBO turn author Matt Ruff’s 2016 novel of the same name into a series that defied any simplistic genre categorization.

The story of Lovecraft Country follows Jonathan Majors’ Tic Freeman, who returns to the US in the aftermath of the Korean War to search for his missing father in the Jim Crow South. Joined by Jurnee Smollett’s Leti, Tic encounters both the terrifying cosmic horrors of HP Lovecraft’s writings and the more banal human horrors of racial segregation, discrimination, and lynching on his perilous journey.

A Deep South travelog, a grim period drama, a character study about grief and loss, a Lovecraftian horror complete with monstrous ageless beings, a dark fantasy about magic, and a sci-fi series all at once, Lovecraft Country can’t be considered any one genre at any given time. Whenever HBO’s adaptation leans into one side of the source story, the next scene or episode will change up its plot again, switching from terrifying paranormal monsters to human antagonists, or from sweet moments of character building to horrific violence.

Compared to hit horror shows of the same era, like Netflix’s critically acclaimed Marianne, which also flirted with Lovecraftian themes, Lovecraft Country was a hard show to pin down. The character study of the show’s slower moments is deeply felt and believable, but the scale of its cosmic horror is just as memorable as the show’s quieter scenes.

Meanwhile, Lovecraft Country’s meta-engagement with its titular co-creator makes the show’s story even more complex. Although the writer is arguably one of the most influential US horror authors of all time, alongside Shirley Jackson, Edgar Allan Poe, and Stephen King, Lovecraft was also a notoriously unapologetic racist whose views were considered retrograde and offensive even during his lifetime.

A lot of Lovecraft’s incredibly influential work features the racism and bigotry found in his personal letters, which has inevitably shaded how readers engage with his writings. Thus, HBO’s Lovecraft Country is also attempting the impressive feat of turning a racist author’s creations into a way to express the anxieties and experiences of a group of Black characters, alongside the rest of the show’s genre-blending experimentation.

It is a big ask, but one that Lovecraft Country pulls off with panache. A lesser show might not have known how to turn a single book into a character drama, a dark fantasy, a cosmic sci-fi, a gruesome horror, and a road trip story, but Lovecraft Country managed to make this blend look easy.

#3416. GTA 6 Cast List: Who plays Jason, Lucia and More

Grand Theft Auto 6 has the longest story ever seen in a GTA game, which also means that it has an enormous cast of characters. Between rival faction leaders, radio station DJs, and fictional rappers, you're going to meet a whole lot of people in Leonida. And some of their voices might sound very familiar.

While the full cast list is so large that it takes up a good chunk of GTA 6's hour-plus end credits, these are some of the biggest players in the story, including Jason and Lucia. Some you might recognize from movies or even previous Rockstar games, while others have some modest TV credits to their name.

Below, we've listed all the actors who play main roles in GTA 6, along with their previous work that they've starred in.

Much of GTA 6's cast comes from a TV background, and that includes Jason Duval. His voice actor, Dylan Rourke, has appeared on shows like 9-1-1: Lone Star, Station 19, and Grey's Anatomy. GTA 6 is his most high-profile role by a mile, though, unless you count his gig as ”Big Guy” on Modern Family as a star turn.

Manni L. Perez, the actress behind Lucia Caminos, comes from a similar acting background as Dylan Rourke. Perez has popped up in Law & Order: Special Victims Unit, Chicago P.D., and The Blacklist. She's also a Rockstar alumni; Perez voices a Clubber in Grand Theft Auto 5, and a Blackjack Dealer in GTA Online.

Jason and Lucia's comedic sidekick is one of the biggest stars in the entire cast. He's voiced by Bobby Moynihan, who was a principal cast member of Saturday Night Live from 2008 to 2017. You may remember him as playing Drunk Uncle, a recurring character on Weekend Update that already felt like a GTA bit. Moynihan has a long credits list outside of that, most recently appearing in NCIS: Origins, The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins, and Minions & Monsters.

The worst kept secret in all of gaming, Stephen Root plays Brian Heder, Jason's employer. He needs little introduction. Root is the man behind Milton in Office Space, Monroe Fuches in Barry, and Bill in King of the Hill, to name a few of his roles. Funny enough, Root is also credited as Florida Man on the TV series It's Florida, Man. Fitting, no?

A standout in the cast, Dre'Quan plays a major supporting role in GTA 6 once the story gets to Vice City. He's played by Naiqui Macabroad, an actor who has appeared on Law & Order, Chicago P.D., and Crashing. Macabroad spends a lot of time in the story acting alongside of Hood Brat and Krissy Celess, two Florida-based rappers who appear in the game.

If you want to see the full credits, including the developers and music, you don't have to beat GTA 6 to get them. Head into the Settings menu from the pause screen and tab over to Account. Scroll down to Credits, and you'll be able to scan a QR code that takes you to the credits on a browser. If you want to skip all of that, here's a direct link to the credits.
