#3414. 10 Shows Like 'The Traitors' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

What started as De Verraders way back in 2021 has become a global reality phenomenon: Peacock in the U.S. hosts the American version with the sartorially supreme Alan Cumming, and also the earlier UK take as well as iterations from Australia, Canada, and New Zealand—but there are spin-offs in France, India, Germany, Ireland, Turkey, and more. Basically, throw a dart at a map and you're likely to hit a country with its own take on The Traitors. And yet! The addictive nature of reality TV means that we can't really ever get enough. In that spirit, here's more backbiting reality TV, and a couple of dramas that offer up similarly duplicitous thrills.

A reality show with a complex history as relates to The Traitors, the premise being so similar that it may well have served as an inspiration. Here, players participate in collaborative missions in order to build a prize fund. But it's not all fun and games: There's a secret double agent among the group (the mole, obviously) whose sole task is to undermine the ability of the rest of the group to earn money. Eliminations are done via quiz: The group is grilled on the information they've collected about the mole, and whoever knows the least gets the boot. Originally airing in the aughts, Netflix brought it back for a couple of seasons more recently, with the potential for more to come. Stream the most recent seasons of The Mole on Netflix.

If there were a prize for dramatic title (and set design), you could do a lot worse than this one. In this South Korean reality show, 12 celebrity contestants are challenged to build a prize pot through strategy games. Sometimes they're collaborative, sometimes entirely competitive, and sometimes a blend, but prizes come in the form of "Pieces" that can be won or lost (and that eventually combine to create their own final puzzle). Anyone who finds themselves without a single Piece is out. Pieces can be spent to buy advantages, and also traded, so the show turns on players forming alliances in order to build the prize pot and survive as long as possible. Stream The Devil's Plan on Netflix.

Here, a bunch of strangers are holed up in an apartment building, cut off from the outside world—and each other. Players can only interact via a custom app, and, thus, can portray themselves however they want, whether that means being 100% genuine (unlikely!) or creating a whole new persona. Players judge the competition based on their interactions, determining the "Influencers" who will get to decide on the eliminations. The show ran for seven seasons on Netflix, and is moving to Hulu for the forthcoming eighth. Stream The Circle on Hulu.

You show up at a fancy hotel, and someone hands you a suitcase containing one million dollars. It's yours to keep—as long as you can keep it a secret. In this one, all the contestants get a suitcase, and only one contains the money. Much as with The Traitors, the goal is to figure out who's keeping the secret, with challenges designed to help flush that person out. If the truth is discovered via a vote, that former millionaire is ousted and the money is concealed in another suitcase until the final contestants are given the opportunity to swap bags with someone who they think has the money. Easy come, easy go, I guess. Stream Million Dollar Secret on Netflix.

I'm a little more into the normies on Traitors myself, but there's no question that a big part of the appeal (for most seasons) is watching reality-show celebs go at it with cash on the line. So it is with House of Villains, a Big Brother-style competition with Joel McHale as ringmaster. The core premise is pretty simple: villains (Richard Hatch, Tom Sandoval, Jonny Fairplay, one-time Trump bestie Omarosa Newman, etc.) compete in challenges for rewards and for safety from the inevitable banishment. It's all mostly an excuse to watch some of TV's biggest personalities go for each other's jugulars. Stream House of Villains on Peacock.

This is not a reality show, but rather a drama about a reality show that may well slake your thirst for treachery while offering up consequences a bit more dramatic than the bruised egos and hurt feelings of The Traitors. Here, eight strangers are selected to compete in a game in which they're locked together in a building and sequestered on different floors each night. They earn money for each minute they last in the game, but all their provisions must be purchased with money they've won, at an extreme markup. At first, the contestants pool their resources so that everyone gets more money—until they learn that people on higher floors are getting more. Then things get nasty Stream The 8 Show on Netflix.

This one plays a bit like The Traitors in reverse: A $250,000 prize pot is, right off the bat, allocated to all 11 contestants who get to hang out in a luxurious villa. So the game isn't about winning money so much as it is about how much you'll keep and how much you're willing to share. Eliminations offer the opportunity to remove those who the others don't want to share with—though contestants don't have to actually ever vote anyone out. They can just keep their portion of the money and hang out, something that obviously does not happen. Challenges along the way force contestants to reveal embarrassing and sometimes ugly truths about themselves that may well put them on the outs with the others. There's only one season at present, though there's potential for more. Stream The Trust on Netflix.

Blending the Big Brother-esque social aspects of Traitors with Survivor's love of the great outdoors, this one drops four teams of four into the Alaskan wilderness (moving to Panama for season three). The contestants are all, by inclination, loners, but the game has only one core rule: Only a team (of at least two) can win, so while the game has the typical reality show eliminations, these wilderness enthusiasts must work together in order to take the money. In the same way that The Traitors creates a tension between competition and cooperation via its communal prize pot, Outlast sees its contestants forced to maintain relationships whether they like it or not. Stream Outlast on Netflix.

The tasks on Traitors aren't typically the most thrilling part of the show, which makes this James Bond-branded competition a solid match if you want more complicated and better developed challenges. In this one, nine teams of two visit exotic locations in each episode and compete in spy-themed activities with the ultimate goal of winning £1 million by making it to the end. It leaves out the bits where people sit around a castle strategizing, but it includes, like Traitors, a dapper Scotsman not afraid to camp it up—in this case, Brian Cox, serving as the spymaster who directs the teams in their missions. Stream 007: Road to a Million on Prime Video.

Squid Game: The Challenge would probably be a more reasonable choice for this list—given that it's a proper reality show and not a blood-chilling thriller. But I'm sticking with the original drama here since, as perfectly entertaining as that spin-off is, it feels like it misses the point. In the original (surprise smash hit) drama, 454 needy contestants are recruited for a new reality competition in which they're tasked to play rather simple children's games—with deadly consequences that are cheered on by the wealthy financiers who are willing to pay good money to watch both the poors go at each other, as people turn on each other to survive and to win the rather shockingly large prize. A bit like The Traitors if all of Alan's murder schtick were literally true. Stream Squid Game on Netflix.

#3413. ‘Artificial’ Trailer: Andrew Garfield Stuns in Luca Guadagnino’s Sharp, Shocking, Funny Portrayal of OpenAI CEO Sam Altman

Luca Guadagnino takes on — and potentially takes down — artificial intelligence and one of its figureheads with his latest feature film, “Artificial.”

A swishy, swively, veering-toward-camp Andrew Garfield plays gay OpenAI CEO Sam Altman opposite an ensemble that includes Oscar-nominated “Anora” breakout Yura Borisov as his former chief scientific officer Ilya Sutskever, Monica Barbaro as erstwhile OpenAI chief technology officer Mira Murati, Ike Barinholtz as an outré Elon Musk, along with Cooper Hoffman, Mark Rylance, Jason Schwartzman, Chris O’Dowd, and Zosia Mamet.

Ahead of the film’s release from Neon on Christmas Day, watch the trailer below. Related Stories ‘The Comeback King’ Trailer: Glen Powell Is a Cancelled Country Star in Judd Apatow’s Latest Directing Project ‘Gentle Monster’ Review: Léa Seydoux Learns the Truth About Her Husband in Marie Kreutzer’s Tough Study of Child Sex Abuse

Written by former “Saturday Night Live” scribe Simon Rich, “Artificial” dramatizes a two-decade artificial intelligence arms race. AI-pioneering professor Geoffrey Hinton makes a vanguard discovery that will change the course of humanity forever — with Sam Altman, Elon Musk, and more prominent Silicon Valley techbros racing to get in on the vision, inevitably leading to corruption that Guadagnino details with scary prescience. Especially as Ilya falls deeper and deeper under Sam Altman’s frighteningly charismatic sway.

As IndieWire’s David Ehrlich previously wrote, “Guadagnino is exploring how difficult it is to abandon the body in the first place — and not just the body, but the intangible essence that it contains. We couldn’t leave it behind if we tried, and this, in his own way, is Guadagnino trying just as hard to do that as Sam Altman ever did.”

“Artificial” was something of an industry hot potato for a sizable stint over the summer, with Amazon MGM Studios dropping the film (which it produced) allegedly over its own ties to artificial intelligence and Altman. Neon eventually picked up “Artificial,” marking the indie company’s first partnership with the “Call Me by Your Name” and “Challengers” director, whose last movie was “After the Hunt,” also at Amazon MGM Studios. “Artificial” surprise-premiered at the New York Film Festival to strong praise — the same week that Aaron Sorkin’s “The Social Network” sorta-sequel “The Social Reckoning” failed to generate much noise.

Neon will take the film into wide release over the Christmas holiday. It’s indeed one of the most crowd-pleasing (and also darkest) films of Guadagnino’s career. (Earlier in December, IndieWire Honors will celebrate the film’s cast at our December 3 event.)

#3412. Five Things I Wish I'd Known Before Getting a Foldable Phone

The iPhone Duo might be the highest profile foldable phone to date, but it’s by no means the first. Personally, I’ve had my eye on the Google variant, the Pixel 11 Pro Fold—and recently I finally took the plunge. I thought I’d done my research to know how different having a foldable phone would be, but I still had a bit to learn. Here are some of the things I wish I’ve learned along the way after making the jump to foldables.

One of the most notable aspects of the iPhone Duo is how wide its screen is, even while closed. And there’s a good reason for that: The larger screen while open has exactly the same 1.41:1 aspect ratio as the smaller screen while closed. This has a ripple effect on how every app you use looks and feels—and whether you like Apple’s approach is largely a matter of personal preference.

Compare with my Pixel 11 Pro Fold, which features an extremely tall 2.17:1 aspect ratio when closed, but a nearly square 1:04:1 aspect ratio when open. On the outer screen, apps are a little less wide than on my old phone, but there’s plenty of space for reading books or articles on the inner screen.

I like the tall, thin display personally because it feels easier to reach buttons with my thumb, and the wider display is better for reading. However, this approach can occasionally result in some odd app layouts. Not every app is designed for tablets, especially on Android, and shifting the aspect ratio between the inner and outer display sometimes means re-rendering or even restarting an app entirely to load properly.

The iPhone Duo has a more consistent aspect ratio and general feel between the inner and outer display, but it comes at the cost of a really wide phone. Neither approach is better or worse on its own, but it might be worth going to a local store to get your hands on the phone you’re thinking about before buying.

For years, the screens on most smartphones have been made of increasingly tough and scratch-resistant glass. So tough that you might not even need a screen protector anymore. On a foldable phone, that can be true of the outside display, but it’s very much not when it comes to the inner, foldable display.

Screens might be foldable, but the strong, durable glass that makes your phone so scratch-resistant isn’t. No matter what foldable phone you use, the covering on the inner display will be more flexible, and thus softer. Apple uses a nano-texture polymer film that can be replaced, but the film on most foldable phones cannot. That means if they get damaged or scratched, those marks will be there for the life of your phone.

If you (like me) haven’t considered a screen protector in a while, it might be time to try one again, at least for the inner display. It’s also worth keeping in mind how rough you plan to be with your phone. Construction sites or factories might not be the best home for a foldable phone you plan to open a lot, but an office job should be a bit safer.

Similar to the screen protector issue, cases can be more of a headache. Most rigid cases will come in two pieces, and the piece that covers the outer display can be shockingly minimal—barely more than a frame, for some of the cases I looked at. A poorly made case can be brittle or pop off more easily, so it’s more important to get a high-quality one.

If you like to use your phone case as your wallet, it’s also important to be wary of cases that aren’t specifically designed for your model of phone (and maybe some that are). A lot of wallet cases are built to unfold to reveal your phone’s screen on one side, and your cards and ID on the other. But depending on how your foldable phone unfolds, it could be awkward to reach the inner screen.

The hinge also introduces more spaces for dust and debris to get into your phone. Despite the extra moving parts and gaps, most foldable phones still offer the now-standard IP68 dust and water resistance rating. That mainly applies to what can get inside and damage the components inside your phone. It’s still possible for hair and dirt to get gummed up in any pinchable spaces, so look out for any case that might provide even more nooks for dust to collect in.

I’ve set up most of my apps how I like them by now, but when I first got my foldable phone, I had to revisit some settings I thought I was done messing with. One of the most notable examples was my ebook apps: I was previously using a single-column, medium-font layout, but it looked ridiculous on the inner display. After switching to a two-column layout, it not only felt more natural, but a lot like reading a regular book.

Similarly, there were some uses for my calendar app that got a whole lot more useful. I’ve never really been able to use anything other than either the one-day or Schedule view if I want to make out anything, but on the inner screen, I can finally look at my week at a glance. But that meant tweaking some things—like showing reminders, which fit naturally amid my events in Schedule view, but become a cluttered mess when I saw 14 different reminders to take my meds at once in the Week view.

Most apps do a decent job of automatically adjusting to different screen sizes, but I found a few outliers that I had to figure out myself. As an example, Google Docs would default to a view with extremely tiny text when I first started using it. It took me a bit to figure out that this was due to a “Print layout” toggle in the document’s settings. This is, for some reason, enabled by default when opening a document on the larger inner screen. It can take some time to learn the eccentricities of all your apps, but it’s worth poking around when you can.

I know, it sounds so obvious, right? The outer screen is the one you’ll use most often, so how could you forget about it? But when you unfold the inner screen, the outer one is still useful in some surprising ways that I hadn’t even considered until I went poking around in some of my apps.

One of the most adorable examples is the Made You Look feature in the Pixel’s Camera app. When unfolded, you can take a picture using the rear camera and see a preview like normal, while the outer screen shows silly animations to capture the attention of a baby or toddler that you want to look into the camera. Admittedly, this is an older feature, but it’s a clever one. For adults, you can also use the outer display to get a selfie preview while using the rear-facing camera.

The outer screen is also just better for some things. YouTube is one of the few apps that has a unique layout designed for a partially folded screen, with the video playing on the tilted-up portion of the screen, and video controls on the bottom portion.

However, in my experience, it was a lot nicer to watch a YouTube video by just propping up the outer screen by unfolding the phone a bit, like a kickstand. My Pixel even detected when YouTube was in full-screen mode on the outer display and would be more forgiving of unfolding the phone without switching to the inner screen. The phone anticipated I might just want to prop up the smaller screen, which I thought was a nice touch.

#3411. All Cheat Codes in GTA 6

The best part about any Grand Theft Auto game is the cheats, and Grand Theft Auto 6 delivers on that front. Rockstar's latest includes a whole mess of password-protected secrets that will really let you have some fun in Vice City. You'll have to work for them, though. GTA 6's cheats are deeply hidden, and will require you to jump through a few hoops to start using them.

Here's everything you need to know about cheats in GTA 6, from how to unlock them, to the list itself.

[Ed. note: We're still working to hunt down every cheat code, but until we find them all, this will give you an idea of what you'll need to do to unlock them all.]

If you're looking for a way to enter cheat codes the moment you start GTA 6, you're going to be disappointed. You won't be able to use them until you have fully cleared the story. Once you finish the game and return to your save file, you'll find a new Cheat tab. Open your Map, tab over to Progression, and scroll to the end to find the Cheats menu.

You won't get the actual cheat codes immediately. Each one is locked behind a requirement. That can be as simple as finding a specific car to earn the ability to summon it, or as demanding as having Jason and Lucia hold hands for four hours. Once you clear a condition, a pop-up message will tell you that you've unlocked a new Cheat code, and the unlock requirement in the Cheats menu will be replaced with the code.

Notably, your progress throughout the game, even before beating it, does contribute to these requirements. By the time you roll credits and unlock the Cheats menu, you'll likely already have a few of them unlocked.

To activate a cheat code, first pull out your phone by pressing Up on your D-Pad. Then hold down L1 and R1 on the home screen. (We have only been able to test the PS5 version of the game so far, but our assumption is that you'll need to hold LB and RB on Xbox Series X.) While holding those buttons, you'll have to enter the unlocked code with the D-Pad. Based on our testing, you won't be able to activate a code until you've actually beaten the game and unlocked the Cheats menu.

Note that activating a cheat code will disable saving for the rest of your play session. You also won't be able to earn achievements while cheats are on. Always remember to save before activating a cheat so you don't lose any progress.

GTA 6's cheats are broken out into five categories:

Below, we've listed every cheat along with their effect, unlock condition, and code.

Complete 50 skydives or base jumps from 300 feet or higher

Get 1st place in 10 races at Gellhorn Raceway, Thrillbilly Mud Club, and Boone Speedway

Nitrous and fuel never runs out on vehicles

Win 25 bronze medals or higher at shooting ranges

Down, Up, Right, Down, Left, Left, Up, Up, Down, Left

Win 25 silver medals or higher at shooting ranges

Ammo never runs out with no need to reload

Adds all explosive weapons to your loadout with full ammo

Adds a Mason & Keen Shortstraw to your loadout that fires explosive shells

Bullets and melee attacks launch targets on impact

Down, Up, Left, Left, Right, Down, Down, Up, Right

Discover the Interstate Ambulance in the Progress menu

Discover the MTL Pumper in the Progress menu

Left, Up, Right, Down, Left, Right, Right, Up

Discover the HVY Bulldozer in the Progress menu

#3410. GTA 6's Best Weapons For Avoiding Police

Grand Theft Auto 6 is finally here, offering players the most immersive experience Rockstar has ever presented. Naturally, that comes with some pros and cons, since realism can sometimes get in the way of running from the cops, but overall, you can still expect to see some wacky and weird stuff across Leonida. As with previous GTA games, you're bound to have police chasing you at some point. GTA 6's map is massive, though, and if you really want to avoid police at all costs, then certain weapons can help you do that better than others.

You'll come across some weapons in the main story missions, and others while taking part in side missions. Other weapons you can buy, upgrade, and customize at Ammu -Nation. There are basically three broad weapon types in GTA 6: owned weapons have a blue icon, unowned weapons have a white icon, and unique weapons have a golden handgun icon. Owned weapons are those purchased at the Ammu-Nation store.

The more you buy from Ammu-Nation, the more options you'll unlock as you progress through the main story. Weapons, body armor, and more can be purchased at Ammu-Nation stores across Leonida. This also includes items that allow you to modify your weapons, which include grips, magazines, muzzle attachments, optics, and suppressors.

Check out all of our guides for GTA 6 here.

In order to customize and upgrade most weapons, you'll have to visit an Ammu-Nation store. However, some items like flashlights you can remove and fix onto your weapon while on the go. Based on what we've seen, the inventory varies depending on the location of the Ammu-Nation store and the size of the store itself.

While we haven't found the single best weapon for helping you avoid police, we have found the best type of weapon. This is mostly related to police response times, which will differ based upon the crime being committed in GTA 6. For instance, crimes against a gang has a slower response time than if you're assaulting some random person on the street, in broad daylight, and with plenty of witnesses.

The best weapons to help you go unnoticed by police in GTA 6 are ones that use suppressors to silence the weapon. Without sound, people won't call the police unless they see you commit the crime. In theory, this means you can use silenced weapons while staying hidden and never have to worry about police being notified.

This is, of course, Grand Theft Auto 6, so if you get a large police tail after you, don't stress too much. It's bound to happen at some point, no matter how much you try to obey laws in the game. And even if you're using a silenced weapon, if someone sees you, the odds are high that the police will be after you soon, no matter how much noise you avoid making.

#3409. 6 Books From the Year 2024 That Are 10/10 Masterpieces

Feel free to connect with him or check out his work. He's everywhere — Upwork, YouTube, Spotify, SoundCloud, Collider, LinkedIn, Instagram.

There’s a bench near my house where I like to read in the evenings. It’s not comfortable, and the light fades fast, but you got to do what you got to do. Last year, I spent more evenings on that bench than I’d like to admit, usually telling myself “just one more chapter” until it got too dark to see the page.

2024 was a strong year for books I’ll be honest, and that made this list harder than I expected. I kept changing the order, moving one book up and another down, then changing it back again. In the end, I went with my gut. These are the six books I kept thinking about long after I closed them, the ones I pushed into my friends’ hands and said, “Just read it, trust me.” So, here they are.

Peter and Ivan Koubek are brothers who have just lost their father, and they don’t really know how to talk to each other. Peter is 32, a successful lawyer in Dublin, stuck between his first love, Sylvia, and Naomi, a much younger student. Ivan is 22, a shy chess player who falls for Margaret, an older woman he meets at a chess event in a small town. Intermezzo follows both brothers as grief quietly messes with every part of their lives.

Sally Rooney, who gave us Normal People, tries something new here. Peter’s chapters are messy and broken, like thoughts racing at 2 a.m., while Ivan’s are slow and careful, just like him. It takes a few pages to get used to, but then it clicks. Besides all the love triangles, this is really a book about two brothers who are trying to find their way back to each other.

It’s August 1975, and a girl goes missing from a summer camp in the Adirondack Mountains. Her name is Barbara Van Laar, she’s 13, and her rich family owns the camp. The scary part is that this has happened before. Fourteen years earlier, Barbara’s older brother, Bear, also disappeared in the same woods and was never found. The God of the Woods jumps between different people and different years as everyone tries to figure out what really happened.

Liz Moore juggles a lot of characters here, from a nervous camp counselor to a young female investigator nobody takes seriously. Somehow, she never drops a single thread. It’s a mystery, sure, but it’s also about money, power, and how rich families hide their secrets. The ending pulls everything together so neatly that I wanted to flip back to page one and start again.

A 45-year-old artist in Los Angeles plans a big road trip to New York, alone, to prove something to herself. But she only drives about 30 minutes before checking into a plain little motel. Then she never leaves. She spends a ridiculous amount of money redecorating her room and falls hard for Davey, a much younger man who works at a car rental place. Meanwhile, her husband and child think she’s halfway across the country.

All Fours is weird, funny, and sometimes so honest it makes you blush. Miranda July writes about getting older, especially what middle age does to a woman’s body and mind, in a way few writers dare to. The book was a finalist for the 2024 National Book Award, and it sparked a lot of loud group chats among women everywhere. You might cringe a little, but you won’t be bored for a second.

Most of us know The Adventures of Huckleberry Finn by Mark Twain, where a boy named Huck runs away down the Mississippi River with Jim, an enslaved man. James tells the same journey, but this time through Jim’s eyes. And the first big surprise is that Jim is clever, well-read, and only talks in a “simple” way around white people to keep himself safe. Among his own people, he speaks perfectly well.

Percival Everett, whose novel Erasure became the film American Fiction, turns a classic upside down and makes it feel brand new. The book is funny in places, which you won’t expect, but it’s also brutal and heartbreaking. It won the 2024 National Book Award for Fiction and later the 2025 Pulitzer Prize. Once you read it, you’ll never see the original the same way again, and honestly, that’s the whole point.

In 1965, Frankie McGrath was a sheltered 20-year-old nursing student from California. When her brother ships off to Vietnam, she makes a bold choice and joins the Army Nurse Corps. Nothing prepares her for what she finds there. Endless injuries, terrible losses, and friendships that keep her going. But the real shock comes later, when she returns home and finds that America doesn’t want to hear about women who served in the war.

Kristin Hannah, the author of The Nightingale, knows exactly how to break your heart, and she does it slowly. The Women is a big, emotional book, and I cried more than once (okay, a lot). What makes it special is that it shines a light on women who were pushed out of the war’s story for decades. Keep tissues nearby, because you’ll need them.

Phoebe Stone shows up at a fancy hotel in Newport, Rhode Island, in her best green dress. She’s sad, lonely, and has quietly planned for this to be her last trip. But there’s a problem. The whole hotel has been booked for a week-long wedding, and she’s the only guest who isn’t part of it. Soon, the bride, Lila, finds out why Phoebe is there, and the two strangers get tangled up in each other’s lives.

It sounds like a dark setup, but The Wedding People is one of the warmest, funniest books I read all year. Alison Espach handles Phoebe’s pain with care, and never makes fun of it. Instead, she shows how a bunch of noisy, annoying strangers can pull someone back toward life without even meaning to. I finished it with a smile, a few tears, and a strange urge to hug someone.

Four of the largest communities on the planet, and four completely different reasons to belong to one. Here is yours, what it would give you, and the argument you would be having within a week.

You belong to the fandom that is really about comfort. Hogwarts works on people because it is a place rather than a plot, and the pull is not the wizard war so much as the corridors, the food, the weather and the sense that somebody is expecting you.

You belong to the deepest fandom on this list, the one where somebody has always read further than you and is quietly delighted to say so. Middle-earth rewards patience more than any other world in popular culture.

You belong to the loudest and largest tent of the four, the one where three generations are all watching the same thing and none of them agree about any of it. That disagreement is not a flaw in this fandom, it is the main activity.

You belong to the thinking fandom, the one that turns up for the argument rather than the explosion. Trek has always been a series of ethical problems in space, and the people who love it love being asked what they would have done.

#3408. Jim Cummings Wakes Up to a Post-One-Night-Stand Crisis in ‘DISC’ — Watch the Short

It’s rare for a short film to be named one of IndieWire’s favorite movies of the fall festival season. But last year, we couldn’t resist adding “DISC” to our roundup of must-see films. Directed by rising filmmaker Blake Winston Rice (who previously made “Tea” with Michael Gandolfini, another short that we championed) and co-written by Victoria Ratermanis, the film premiered at the 2025 Toronto International Film Festival before screening at more than 50 festivals worldwide. Now, just in time for the Best Live Action Short race, IndieWire can debut the full film as this month’s Vimeo Staff Pick.

“DISC” stars Ratermanis and indie filmmaker Jim Cummings as two conference attendees whose drunken hookup turns them into unexpected partners in crime when an inexplicable twist of fate turns their world upside down the following morning. We won’t spoil the unique premise, but an official synopsis reads: “After a one-night stand during a work conference, a man and woman wake to an unexpected crisis. With a career-defining presentation looming, the two near-strangers must navigate an uncomfortably intimate situation and the fragile connection it reveals.” Related Stories ‘Artificial’ Trailer: Andrew Garfield Stuns in Luca Guadagnino’s Sharp, Shocking, Funny Portrayal of OpenAI CEO Sam Altman ‘The Comeback King’ Trailer: Glen Powell Is a Cancelled Country Star in Judd Apatow’s Latest Directing Project

Following its TIFF premiere, “DISC” went on to play at the 2026 Tribeca Festival, where it reportedly caused audiences to faint in multiple screenings. Other festival bows included the Clermont-Ferrand International Short Film Festival, Woodstock Film Festival, Indy Shorts, and the Palm Springs International ShortsFest.

Cummings is best known for writing, directing, and starring in the 2018 SXSW breakout “Thunder Road,” which he followed with the features “The Wolf of Snow Hollow” and “The Beta Test.” He also continues to act in projects for other filmmakers, including recent roles in “The Last Stop in Yuma County” and “Redux Redux.” He can also be seen in theaters later this month as Oliver Babcock in “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.”

Rice’s other short film credits include “Sawdust,” “Steps,” and “The Recovery Call.” He is currently developing his first feature, “The Empty Lot.”

#3407. The Unexpected History of 'Black Friday'

Since the 1950s, Black Friday—once simply known as "the day after Thanksgiving"—has grown into a quasi-holiday in the United States marked by steep discounts, ceaseless shopping, and occasional violence. But more recently, Black Friday has also metastasized. It's not a day anymore. It's a week, a month, a veritable state of mind. (Speaking of which, check out Lifehacker's Black Friday coverage. We got all the deals, baby!)

While pre-dawn trips to the mall are waning as online shopping grows, in-person shopping on Black Friday is still a big deal in the U.S.—it’s estimated that around 80 million Americans visited a brick-and-mortar store on Black Friday in 2025. But how did Black Friday come about, and what does it all mean?

“Black Friday” in the United States originally referred to the start of the Panic of 1869, when the collapse of the price of gold devastated the national economy. “Black Friday” as a description of the day after Thanksgiving dates back to 1951; the term first appeared in the journal Factory Management and Maintenance, where it referred to the number of employees who skipped work on the day after Thanksgiving. Around the same time, the police in Philadelphia and Rochester started informally using “Black Friday” to describe the traffic and crowds that appeared in their cities as shoppers hit the stores on the day after Thanksgiving. The phrase gradually caught on. It was picked up by national press in 1975 when the New York Times used "Black Friday" specifically to describe the day after Thanksgiving and the shopping and sales it brings.

But even before it had a name, Black Friday was a thing. The day after Thanksgiving has been known by merchants as the start of the shopping season since the late 1800s. By the early 20th century, retailers sponsored Thanksgiving Day parades that traditionally ended with an appearance by Santa Claus, as if to say, “Now it’s time to shop for Christmas.” By unspoken agreement among retailers, Christmas-themed advertisements rarely appeared before Thanksgiving in our grandparents’ day. This informal bargain obviously no longer applies.

Referring to a day as “black” traditionally denotes a period of calamity or tragedy, leading some to suggest different names for the day. In the early 1960s, Philadelphia merchants suggested “Big Friday,” a name which did not catch on, leaving retailers with the weak explanation that the “black” in Black Friday refers to the black ink denoting profits in a ledger. Oft-repeated lore suggests that retailers are "in the red" all year, and only start making an annual profit at the end of the year, but big retail chains generally make money all year long.

A more modern issue with the name is that Black Friday sales now last for days or even weeks, beginning in early to mid-November and bleeding over into the following Saturday, Sunday, “Cyber Monday,” Tuesday, and beyond, leading people to say things like, “Do you want to go Black Friday shopping this Sunday?” So far, alternative names like “Five-Day Frenzy” and “The day I get to trample someone to save $8 on a Nespresso” haven’t caught on. But here’s hoping.

Beginning around 2010, an insatiable thirst for profits led many retailers to push the start of Black Friday shopping to Thursday (aka Thanksgiving Day). Kmart opened Thanksgiving morning. Toys R Us opened that night. By 2011, Walmart was opening its doors at 10 p.m. on Thursday. The trend led to widespread backlash, with many Americans appalled that employees were forced to work on Thanksgiving or angry that consumerism was encroaching upon a holiday meant to celebrate colonialism. By 2021, most major retailers had relented and elected to remain closed on Thanksgiving.

The term “Cyber Monday” describes the boost in online retail sales on the Monday after Thanksgiving, sparked by workers returning to the office and getting right to online shopping. The term first appeared on Nov. 28, 2005, in a Shop.org press release entitled “'Cyber Monday’ Quickly Becoming One of the Biggest Online Shopping Days of the Year," which may be the most influential press release ever written. Since its early 2000s birth, Cyber Monday has become the biggest online shopping day of the year. Americans spent $14.25 billion online on Cyber Monday 2025, according to Adobe Analytics. So is Cyber Monday bigger than Black Friday? Retailers really don't care: Analysts now tend to mash everything into the category of "Black Friday–Cyber Monday" (or even "Cyber Week").

If all this naked consumerism makes you a little squeamish, you're not alone. Anti-consumerists have named the day after Thanksgiving “Buy Nothing Day,” which you can celebrate by doing charity work, cutting up your credit cards, or simply not purchasing anything. Pioneered by artist Ted Dave and popularized by Adbusters magazine, the first Buy Nothing Day was celebrated in Canada in 1992.

It’s hard to measure the success of the alternative holiday. Both online and brick-and-mortar retail sales have increased sharply since 1992, suggesting Buy Nothing Day’s effect is negligible. On the other hand, maybe big retailers are losing millions because someone on Bluesky reminded you not to shop. Sure.

Depending on how you measure it, Black Friday has resulted in between one and 17 deaths. Jdimytai Damour is the only person killed directly due to a Black Friday sale: The 34-year-old worker was trampled to death by a surging crowd at a Long Island Walmart on Black Friday in 2008. If you include car accidents, shootings, retail worker suicides, and fatal heart attacks, Black Friday’s death toll balloons to 17, with 128 reported injuries.

Black Friday violence has even inspired a horror flick: Eli Roth's 2023 holiday-themed slasher Thanksgiving opens with a hilariously brutal Black Friday riot at a big box store, setting off a chain of events that involve a lot of people being murdered by a dude in a Pilgrim mask.

I mean, yeah, of course. Critics of Black Friday point out that there are arguably better times to buy a new TV (like the week before the Super Bowl), not to mention plenty of other goods. Savings from Black Friday shopping are often illusory—big-ticket “doorbuster” items generally sell out quickly, leaving behind goods that are, by and large, priced the same as they would be at any other time of year. Some retailers even mark up products ahead of Black Friday so the discounts look bigger. If you're buying online, your browser history, location, and cart contents can tweak the prices you see on Black Friday, as they can on any other day.

Yet despite protest holidays, the unpleasantness of shopping when stores are overcrowded, and the frustration of hunting for bargains that often aren't that great to begin with, Black Friday stubbornly remains an unofficial holiday, celebrated by over 100 million Americans in one way or another. What that says about our country's relationship with capitalism is unclear, but personally, I’m going to continue my own day-after-Thanksgiving tradition of eating pie for breakfast and thinking about going for a walk, but then watching The Quick and the Dead instead. I'm not protesting anything; I just don't need the hassle.

#3406. Walmart’s 2026 Black Friday and Cyber Monday Sales Are Now Live

If you're thinking of picking up any big-ticket items—whether for yourself or as a gift for someone on your list— I would advise you not to sleep on Walmart's sale. Walmart is the first major retailer to announce and kick off its Black Friday and Cyber Monday sale for 2026, and they're actually holding three major shopping events between now and the December holidays.

Walmart will hold three sales between Nov. 12 and Dec. 2, as outlined in a recent press release. The sales will be both online and in-store, and will target a mix of Walmart+ members and general shoppers.

The events will take place on three different dates:

Walmart's Black Friday Deals Event 1: Nov. 12–15

Available online and in stores starting at 6 a.m. local time

Walmart+ members get six hours of early access beginning online at 12:01 a.m. ET on Nov. 12

Walmart's Black Friday Deals Event 2: Nov. 23–29

Online only: Nov. 23 starting at 12:01 a.m. ET

Online and in stores: Nov. 27 starting at 6 a.m. local time

Walmart+ members get six hours of early access online beginning Nov. 23 at 12:01 a.m. ET

Walmart's Cyber Monday Deals Event: Nov. 30-Dec. 2

Walmart's physical stores will open at 6:00 a.m. local time on Nov. 27 for their Black Friday events. Of course, they will start online earlier, so make sure to check their website as well.

Walmart says that they will have discounts on electronics, toys, fashion, beauty, home goods, gifts, and everyday essentials. Although the company doesn't provide much in the way of specifics in its press release, last year's sales included discounts on TCL TVs, Dyson vacuums, Dreo appliances, and toys from LEGO.

Walmart's first sale already features plenty of good deals; you don't need to wait for Nov. 27 to start to find some products going for their lowest prices ever. Here are some of the best ones I've found so far:

No. But if you are a Walmart+ member, you'll get early access to the sale. You can sign up for a free 30-day Walmart+ subscription and cancel it afterwards or get the annual plan for $98 ($8.17/month).

Deals will be both online and in the physical stores. There might be deals online that you won't see in-store and vice versa.

The holiday season will see major sales from the same list of retailers that compete for your dollars throughout the year—namely, Best Buy, Target, and Amazon. Each will have its own version of Black Friday and Cyber Monday sales. So far, only Walmart has revealed its plans.

In short, yes. Though they aren't quite as impactful as they once were, Black Friday and Cyber Monday sales offer discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. Whether it's a major purchase you've been saving up for or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts, especially on items like appliances and electronics. Last year's sales included categories such as tech, home improvement, and fitness.

Black Friday used to be when major retailers offered their best deals on expensive tech and appliances, while Cyber Monday was for cheaper tech and gave smaller businesses a chance to compete online. Now, however, the distinction is almost meaningless: Every major retailer offers sales on both days, which means the smart move is to know what you want, use price trackers to monitor the deals, and refer to our Black Friday coverage, where we do all the searching, curating, and price tracking for you.

#3405. ‘Elsinore’ Review: Andrew Scott’s Towering Performance as a Dying Actor Can’t Overcome AIDS-Movie Awards Bait Clichés

[Editor’s note: This review was originally published on September 5, 2026 during the 2026 Telluride Film Festival. Focus Features will release the film in theaters Friday, November 20.]

There’s no question Andrew Scott, the 49-year-old Irish actor, has earned his position as one of the finest contemporary actors going. He’s in demand, but choosing wisely, and in roles that slyly play off his own status as an out gay man (a rare thing indeed) but with something off-center beneath, often a secret. He played Tom Ripley, one even more sociopathic than Matt Damon’s own iconically calculating Adonis, to devastating effect in the sinister Netflix series “Ripley,” there more explicitly grappling with the Patricia Highsmith character’s ambiguous (but was it?) sexuality. He played the Hot Priest who turned down a chance at heterosexual, secular love in “Fleabag,” of course, and starred in “All of Us Strangers” as a lonely adult orphan living in a glittering tower, bracing himself for romantic intimacy with Paul Mescal. Related Stories Jim Cummings Wakes Up to a Post-One-Night-Stand Crisis in ‘DISC’ — Watch the Short ‘Artificial’ Trailer: Andrew Garfield Stuns in Luca Guadagnino’s Sharp, Shocking, Funny Portrayal of OpenAI CEO Sam Altman

I also saw him playing up to nine roles in Anton Chekhov’s “Vanya” onstage in New York City last year as men and women of all sorts, showing an actor who can shimmy between genders and across ranges. He has the unmistakable warmth of someone you should trust, but with intrigue behind the curtain of many of his performances to suggest that maybe you shouldn’t. He’s that good.

Scott has now taken on what will, to this point, I suppose, go down as “the role of a lifetime” in director Simon Stone’s rueful, pained, and unremarkable new film drama “Elsinore” as Scottish actor Ian Charleson, who died of HIV/AIDS complications while portraying Hamlet at the National Theatre in London in 1990. Charleson’s story is unlikely to be one most are familiar with. Even the most public of deaths among the most publicly gay of people often still remain in hiding, though Charleson wasn’t out himself. He resisted pressures from his inner circle to announce his disease amid a stage run that miraculously lasted 24 performances. Actors then were afraid of damaging their reputations. It’s not that different now, even as many advancements have made HIV/AIDS feel locally like a plague of the past.

A blond-headed Scott throws himself valiantly into the role of Charleson with the urgency and commitment of any of his best work, but the problem isn’t his: It’s that the movie surrounding him dulls the greatness of his performance with its conventional storytelling, and over-complication in post. “Elsinore” is one of those movies where you can feel the filmmaker — here, Stone, known for both stage and screen — actively laboring to “open up the play” with the opportunities of film. But “Elsinore” was never a play. Instead, it’s a movie where every emotional beat worth lingering on, especially Charleson’s swan-song performances as Hamlet, is churned into a frenzied montage of editing that won’t let the material take a breath. Or the audience sink in.

Charleson played an Olympian athlete in the Best Picture-winning 1981 film “Chariots of Fire,” and an Anglican priest in the next year’s Best Picture topper, “Gandhi.” That was after playing an outré bisexual in the 1978 film “Jubilee,” directed by his former lover, the very openly gay director Derek Jarman, who died of AIDS in 1994. Aside from a handful of film credits, including one alluded to in “Elsinore” as Dario Argento’s giallo “Opera,” Charleson otherwise kept to the stage. Scott’s Charleson at one point in this film opines about how much more satisfying stage work is for an actor without an editor there to chop you up to pieces.

Stone, working from a screenplay by Stephen Beresford (himself a playwright), does not follow his protagonist’s lead. Every thoughtful consideration of Kaposi’s sarcoma lesions, or the retching of blood into buckets under the care of dutiful practitioner Dr. Margaret Johnson (Olivia Colman) to show the terrible realities of the disease, is whipped into what feels like a feature-length trailer. The best scenes out of the “Hamlet” production detailed here are tossed into a rushed montage near the movie’s end that gives us no sense of what we are promised is a performance of enormity. (The play in 1990 was directed by Richard Eyre, later the filmmaker behind features like the campy diva battle “Notes on a Scandal.” He’s played in “Elsinore” by Johnny Flynn.)

A couple of things are going on: “Elsinore” triggers in a watchful gay viewer’s senses the signifiers of what would be the AIDS awards-bait movie of serious gravitas. Tom Hanks’ Oscar-winning performance in “Philadelphia.” Ed Harris in “The Hours.” Everyone who came out of the cringey “Dallas Buyers Club” with Academy Awards in 2014. There are others, though more lost to time. We become suspicious of this device, especially when paired with great acting. Is HIV/AIDS being exploited in the package of a would-be Oscar hit? Or are we showing young queer audiences how it was, how we got to where we are, and how where that is still isn’t perfect? It can be both, but the structure of “Elsinore” tips toward the former.

Then, there’s a veritable, cheeky who’s-who of British gay literati and luminaries lingering about “Elsinore’s” 1989 London milieu that’s irresistible in theory, but often drab in execution. There’s Eyre, of course, and Jarman (David Dawson, as excellent and tender and wounded here as he was in his screen breakthrough “My Policeman”). The afterburn of his relationship with Charleson lingers affectingly, though. After some drinks, he invites Charleson home, but they instead part with one of those tacit kisses shared by people who once loved each other but can’t make it work anymore. There’s too much history here. The lingering scorches of Charleson’s secret affairs and friendships with various (and out) men make for the best parts of “Elsinore,” but there’s no life to the telling. (Joe Locke plays a young man also ailing in Johnson’s AIDS clinic alongside Charleson.)

The pallid grayness of Mike Eley’s cinematography is probably supposed to mimic the finality of HIV/AIDS taking hold, but there’s no passion aesthetically to counterbalance what becomes absolute misery onscreen to watch. I’m not in the business of comparing one gay social drama to another, but Robin Campillo’s 2017 Cannes-winning French drama “Beats Per Minute” imbued an albeit more activist-oriented story of ACT UP fighting against AIDS suppression in Paris with such heat and spectacle. Watching someone die of AIDS in a room becomes a bore unless anyone is given a reason to keep on living.

That reason is, of course, supposed to be Charleson’s performance in “Hamlet,” which is relegated to a whirlwind sequence at the movie’s end after many pained rehearsals where he refused to drop out (and where Johnson encouraged him to). Scott has a mesmerizing hold on his scenes, and he’s compelling to watch in his repartee with Colman as Johnson, who treated the disease at a time when it was most stigmatized. She named her groundbreaking HIV testing clinic after him; that’s how much he impacted her. We are told how much Charleson mattered to people, but never shown it. Which unfortunately shuffles off “Elsinore,” named after the Danish town where “Hamlet” was set and where its main character died, off to the realm of HIV/AIDS movies seeking prestige over deep feeling.

“Elsinore” premiered at the 2026 Telluride Film Festival. Focus Features releases it starting November 20.

#3404. 2 Months After GTA 6, Prime Video Drops The Closest Thing To Its Live-Action Series

Grand Theft Auto VI is finally here, and, unsurprisingly, it is already making waves across the globe.

What is surprising, though, is that despite the game series' worldwide reach and long-running legacy, it has not been adapted for the screen yet. Given how the game in itself allows one to have a completely immersive and serialized storytelling experience, pulling off its live-action adaptation will not be an easy feat.

However, considering the growing demand for prestige video game adaptations, a GTA live-action adaptation might eventually see the light of day. While only time will tell whether that will eventually happen, an upcoming crime drama could perfectly qualify as a live-action GTA. Based on Ed Brubaker's comics of the same name, Prime Video's Criminal has many ingredients that would appeal to GTA fans.

While Ed Brubaker's Criminal comics may not be as popular as GTA, they, too, have a solid legacy of their own. They are highly acclaimed and have won multiple accolades. Prime Video's adaptation of the comic series also has a lot going in its favor, and it is set to premiere precisely two months after GTA 6 on January 13, 2027.

Similar to the original comics, Prime Video's Criminal will not follow a single protagonist. Instead, like the recent Grand Theft Auto games, it will switch between the perspectives of many different outlaws whose lives are intertwined through crime.

The show's first season will be split into two four-episode arcs. The first arc, titled "Coward", will center on a cautious but masterful thief named Leo Patterson (Charlie Hunnam).

In Part 2, "Lawless," the series will follow Tracy Lawless (Luke Evans), an AWOL soldier who sets out to investigate his brother's murder. Just like GTA's main characters become main leads in the DLCs, the Criminal comics give enough room to all characters to shine. Some of the best story beats in GTA are also driven by a fully developed crime ecosystem.

The overarching ecosystem involves a diverse set of players, including kingpins, cops, and fixers. Even in Brubaker's Criminal universe, everything from gambling clubs to local bars radiates outwards. The show's character archetypes will also read GTA's mission-giver roster.

Compared to GTA, the Prime Video crime drama will be far grittier in tone and less satirical. In fact, it will likely be completely bereft of the humor that defines the games. However, like GTA, Criminal, too, will completely strip away the romanticism of crime and deliver a realistic portrayal of a generational web of crimes and criminals.

Dan Houser is not only one of the co-founders of Rockstar Games, but he also serves as the lead writer and creative director for most titles in the GTA series. He is best known for his work in games like GTA, Red Dead Redemption, Bully, and Max Payne. However, he also serves as the writer of the acclaimed American Caper comics that are seemingly ripe for adaptation.

In terms of tone, the American Caper comics are even closer to GTA than Criminal with their acidic satire of American access. They also feature some bizarre and unhinged characters in their stories, reminding one of the NPCs from the GTA games. If Prime Video's Criminal proves to be successful, there will certainly be an audience for American Caper's TV adaptation.

A live-action movie or television adaptation of Grand Theft Auto VI may not be completely off the cards. However, it is certainly not happening anytime soon. Even if it does not see the light of day, however, fans of the games can always read comics like Criminal and American Caper and check out their TV adaptations.

Based on the comic series, Criminal is an action crime series developed by Ed Brubaker and Jordan Harper for Prime Video. This adaptation follows various characters within and adjacent to a bustling criminal underworld and comprises several arcs that occasionally intersect. The series was greenlit by Amazon in 2024.

#3403. 5 Essential Harlan Coben TV Shows for Beginners

Every generation has a master of literary mysteries. The modern mystery maker owning that moniker is Harlan Coben. The author of over 35 novels, Coben is known for fast-paced thrillers rooted in twisted mysteries. Having engineered the potboiler formula, giving readers the equivalent of a book binge. Coben's stories almost always start with an ordinary, relatable scenario and ask a simple "what if?" question. These hooks immediately pull readers into a state of high curiosity. His pacing is relentless; the chapters are swift, and with exceptional twists and cliffhangers, they give fans a constant micro-dose of adrenaline.

His work is so rich in fascination that it's become the perfect source material for streamers. His massive global footprint has exploded thanks to a lucrative deal with Netflix, turning his work into sleek, multi-language international event series that have become yearly guilty pleasures for mystery lovers. If you've heard the lore surrounding his thrilling masterpiece shows but have not committed to the dozen-plus titles, we have a beginner’s guide on how to immerse yourself in his enthralling cinematic world. The shows on this list offer a strong mix of narratives, characters, and themes that will help you understand why his work has become so addictive. Whether you figure out the shocks before they're revealed or find yourself gobsmacked by series end, these five series prove why Coben is a defining voice in the mystery genre.

One of the juiciest twist-filled thrillers is Fool Me Once. Based on his 2016 novel, the Netflix series follows Maya Burkett-Stern (Michelle Keegan), a former military pilot grieving the brutal murder of her husband, Joe (Richard Armitage), who is shocked when she spots him alive on her toddler's nanny cam. As she launches a desperate investigation into the impossible sighting—and looks for connections to her sister Claire's (Natalie Anderson) unsolved murder months earlier—she uncovers a web of deadly secrets tied to her wealthy in-laws, namely the family matriarch, Judith Burkett (Joanna Lumley). Meanwhile, Detective Sergeant Sami Kierce (Adeel Akhtar) leads the official homicide case while battling his own demons, colliding with Maya as the truth unravels. A genuinely captivating thrill ride, Fool Me Once captivates audiences through a titillating hook and interconnected conspiracies that keep you on your toes.

Fool Me Once serves as a brilliant entry point for beginners because, while it deals with dark themes like murder and grief, it plays out as an approachable, twist-heavy soap-opera thriller rather than a dense or overly terrifying procedural. Through eight fast-paced episodes, Fool Me Once piles twist upon twist at the end of nearly every episode, creating an addictive, puzzle-box structure where viewers constantly question who to trust. Set against scenic backdrops in North West England and elevated by a tense, atmospheric score, the show delivers high-melodrama thrills with a sensational ensemble. Filled with Coben staples and powerhouse British greats like Dino Fetscher, Fool Me Once is simply delicious.

If you're new to the Coben-Netflix collaboration, each New Year's Day tends to give you a reason to stay in, as the streamer releases a new Coben show every January 1st. For 2026, it was Run Away. In the utterly shocking series, Simon Greene's (James Nesbitt) seemingly perfect life shatters when his eldest daughter, Paige (Ellie de Lange), runs away and spirals into drug addiction. After Simon finally tracks her down busking in a park, a violent altercation with her abusive boyfriend, Aaron Corval (Thomas Flynn), causes Paige to vanish again—shortly before Aaron turns up murdered, making Simon a prime suspect. Determined to rescue his daughter while clearing his name, Simon plunges into a dangerous criminal underworld alongside a tenacious private investigator, uncovering dark cult ties and devastating family secrets along the way. Run Away stands out as a high-stakes mystery thriller for its intense family drama, relentless pacing, and a multi-layered web of secrets that are borderline mind-blowing.

Run Away kicks off with an immediate, high-octane premise. True to Coben's signature style, the narrative weaves together rogue assassins, a mysterious cult, overlapping missing-person cases, and continuous cliffhangers that subvert expectations from episode to episode. Beyond the crime mechanics, the series digs into a resonant psychological theme: how little we truly know about the people closest to us and the hidden traumas families bury. Nesbitt delivers a grounded, desperate performance as Simon, supported by Minnie Driver as his wife, Dr. Ingrid Greene, Alfred Enoch as Detective Sergeant Isaac Fagbenle, and Ruth Jones as private investigator Elena Ravenscroft. One of the best binge-watches of the bunch, Run Away will leave you begging for a second chapter to tackle the shocking aftermath.​​​​​​​

Arriving just before the big collaboration between Netflix and Coben began, Safe was a literal entry point for many intrigued by the author’s work. The 2018 thriller follows widowed pediatric surgeon Tom Delaney (Michael C. Hall) as he frantically searches for his teenage daughter, Jenny (Amy James-Kelly), who vanishes after a house party. As Tom investigates alongside his girlfriend, Detective Sergeant Sophie Mason (Amanda Abbington), the disappearance of Jenny's boyfriend, Chris Chahal (Freddie Thorp), raises the stakes and sparks a wider murder inquiry. Along the way, Tom uncovers a tangled web of lies, blackmail, and dark secrets hidden behind the doors of his seemingly idyllic gated community. Safe is a highly addictive narrative led by a robust performance from an elite star.

Unlike some of Coben's later, more sprawling or coincidence-heavy thrillers, the core mystery—a desperate widowed father searching for his missing teenage daughter in a gated community—is easy to track and root for. Set in an affluent, seemingly secure English gated community, the show thrives on the contrast between outward respectability and the dark, dangerous secrets neighbors, friends, and family harbor. The narrative continuously interweaves multiple mysteries, using steady cliffhangers and misdirection to keep viewers guessing through the finale. Hall brings his signature intense, secretive drive, anchoring the ensemble's compelling interpersonal dynamics. Safe is a thrill-a-minute equivalent television blockbuster with intriguing characters and a tightly woven narrative. ​​​​​​​

Britain makes more detective television than any country has any business making, and somehow almost all of it is good. Here is the one you belong in, what it says about you, and the case for it being the best of the four.

You want the tea, the gossip and the vicar behaving oddly. Midsomer is a county where the scenery is beautiful, the fete is on Saturday and the murder rate is roughly that of a small war, and absolutely nobody involved thinks this is strange.

You feel other people's grief as if it were handed to you personally. Broadchurch is less a whodunnit than a study of what a small town does to itself when it finds out that the answer was always going to be somebody everybody already knew.

You go through things rather than around them. John Luther is the best detective in London and a liability to everybody who works with him, and the show is completely honest that those two facts are the same fact.

You say the thing and you do not dress it up. Vera Stanhope turns up in a hat and a mac, is rude to almost everybody, and is the only person in the room prepared to ask the question that the family has been waiting years for somebody to ask.

A top-tier Coben entry, Stay Close combines classic puzzle-box storytelling with deep psychological tension. The premise centers on three people whose comfortable lives are upended when dark secrets from their past resurface. Suburban mother of three Megan Pierce (Cush Jumbo), washed-up paparazzo Ray Levine (Richard Armitage), and obsessed detective Michael Broome (James Nesbitt) are drawn together after a local man vanishes on the exact anniversary of a 17-year-old cold case. As an old acquaintance delivers shocking news about Megan's buried life as a nightclub dancer, all three must confront a web of lies and serial murders before their pasts destroy everyone they love. Capturing the signature Coben aesthetic, Stay Close neatly packs the author's favorite tropes: ordinary suburban people hiding dark, decades-old secrets, a haunting cold case, and a web of interconnected lies.

Unlike most of the other Coben shows, Stay Close uniquely presents three distinct viewpoints, giving you multiple ways to stay hooked. Aside from the core mystery, the show injects quirky, eccentric, and dark subplots, including a pair of dancing, psychopathic hitmen named Barbie (Poppy Gilbert) and Ken (Hyoie O'Grady), that keep the tone unpredictable. Rather than relying purely on a shock-value twist, the narrative explores the psychological weight of what happens after long-buried secrets resurface and how people live with their past choices. Beyond the main trio, the series features some fabulous British staples, including Sarah Parish and Eddie Izzard. A lightning-fast, bonkers, bingeable thriller, Stay Close grabs you with immediate stakes and standout performances. ​​​​​​​

If you only had time to watch a single Coben show, The Stranger is it. The standout series follows family man Adam Price (Richard Armitage), whose seemingly idyllic suburban life unravels when a mysterious woman (Hannah John-Kamen) reveals a shocking secret about his wife, Corinne (Dervla Kirwan). After Adam confronts her about faking a past pregnancy and miscarriage, Corinne abruptly vanishes without explanation. As Adam desperately searches for his wife and investigates the enigmatic blackmailer, he uncovers a dark, interconnected web of lies, murder, and deceit threatening everyone around him. A gripping, highly addictive mystery thriller, The Stranger's tight structure and high suspense capture you the moment the titular character enters the frame.

Structured as a tight, self-contained 8-episode miniseries, the editing and scripting create urgent momentum that compels viewers to keep watching as they piece the puzzle together. Instead of a single straightforward crime, the show weaves together multiple parallel subplots, including a local police investigation led by DS Johanna Griffin (Siobhan Finneran) and a strange local conspiracy involving a group of teenagers. While it weaves together teenagers, local cops, and suburban families, the script keeps the interwoven secrets clear and fast-paced rather than confusing. These disparate threads gradually collide in perfect Coben fashion. The Stranger boasts one of the strongest ensembles from top to bottom. John-Kamen is absolutely exceptional. Her ability to bring profound strength and magnetism, dropping seeds of intrigue, makes her character one of Coben's strongest. Armitage delivers a grounded, tormented lead performance, supported by a deep British cast, including Jacob Dudman, Anthony Head, Shaun Dooley, Kadiff Kirwan, Stephen Rae, Ritu Arya, and Jennifer Saunders. The Stranger exemplifies the author's trademark suburban paranoia by exposing the dark secrets and hidden lies lurking beneath the surface of seemingly normal neighborhood lives.

#3401. Skydance to Combine Warner Bros. Television Group and Paramount Television Studios as One Big Studio

The corporate shakeups keep coming at Skydance, this time to the TV department. Warner Bros. Television Group and Paramount Television Studios are being combined as one big studio under Skydance, with WB’s Channing Dungey and Paramount’s Matt Thunell serving as presidents of the combined studio.

The new studio, which officially launches in early 2027 (the two entities will keep operating independently until then), will be known as Warner Bros. Television Studios. The entire studio will report to George Cheeks, co-chair and Chief Content Officer of Skydance TV. As previously announced, Dungey also serves as Chair of Skydance Global Cable Media, with oversight over all 50+ WB Discovery and Paramount cable brands. Related Stories IDA Documentary Awards 2026 Nominations: ‘You Can See Everything,’ ‘Concrete Land,’ and More Earn Nods A24’s TV Division Is Quietly Having as Strong a Year as Its Film Team

Together, Dungey and Thunell will lead all of scripted and unscripted programming, overseeing all creative departments. They will also oversee BET Studios and Warner Bros. International Television Production’s studios around the world.

CBS Studios will continue to operate independently, headed by President David Stapf, who also reports to Cheeks. CBS Studios International, Skydance Sports Entertainment and See It Now Studios will operate under the CBS Studios umbrella.

The new Warner Bros. Television Studios will be home to more than 120 active television series and some of the industry’s biggest global franchises, including “Harry Potter and The Philosopher’s Stone” (HBO), “The Pitt” (HBO Max), “Ted Lasso” (Apple TV), “Georgie & Mandy’s First Marriage” (CBS), “Reacher” (Prime Video), “Marshals” (CBS), “Landman” (Paramount+), “Emily in Paris” (Netflix) and the upcoming series “Neuromancer” (Apple TV).

Yesterday, Skydance made some big changes to its film side of the business, appointing Don Granger and Kira Goldberg to lead Paramount’s Motion Picture Group and Jesse Ehrman to lead Warner Bros. Pictures. It also recently shook up DC Studios, with James Gunn and Peter Safran exiting and giving way to Jeremy Latcham.

“Bringing together two of the industry’s most prolific television studios creates a formidable creative engine, uniting extraordinary talent, resources, acclaimed programming and iconic franchises with the global scale to compete at the highest level. With Channing and Matt at the helm, we have two exceptional leaders who understand what it takes to empower creative talent, foster bold ideas and deliver programming that resonates with audiences everywhere,” Cheeks said in a statement. “Alongside CBS Studios, led by the incomparable David Stapf, Warner Bros. Television Studios gives us two world-class studios, with the breadth, depth and creative ambition to deliver for Skydance platforms and third-party partners across the industry.”

“Matt has extraordinary creative instincts, and a deep understanding of great storytelling. I couldn’t ask for a better partner as we bring these storied studios together,” Dungey said in a statement. “We have a unique opportunity to create something truly special for our creative partners and audiences around the world. I’m very excited to begin this new chapter.”

Thunell said, “Channing is one of the most accomplished and respected executives in our industry, with an extraordinary track record of building successful businesses, developing enduring partnerships and delivering some of television’s most acclaimed programming. Ever since our time together at Netflix, I’ve hoped we’d have the opportunity to work together again, and I’m thrilled that day has finally come. We’re bringing an unmatched roster of talent under one roof, building on the remarkable legacies of two storied studios. The possibilities ahead are extraordinary, and I couldn’t be more excited to partner with Channing to champion the ambitions of our creative talent and bring exceptional stories to audiences around the world.”

#3399. All 8 Episodes Of HBO's 'Modern Sopranos' Masterpiece Are Perfect From Start To Finish

HBO Max has a modern Sopranos-like series that has eight episodes that are perfect from start to finish. HBO’s best shows tend to be in the drama genre, with The Sopranos being one of them. Similarly, the iconic show has aged well on HBO, overcoming the possible revisionism that tends to happen with early 2000s products. Several modern projects will likely do the same as time goes on, though revisionism eventually comes for all things.

That said, The Sopranos provides more evidence of aging well than anything else, given that the show is almost 30 years old and still counted among the best TV shows of all time. Whether these aforementioned modern productions will eclipse this reputation remains to be seen, but there are several that emulate The Sopranos in several ways. One such show is a drama that actually exists within another genre first, despite being more like The Sopranos than anything else.

That show is The Penguin, the spin-off to 2022’s The Batman. The show was released in 2024 and focuses on the titular Batman villain, otherwise known as Oz Cobb. Across eight episodes, Oz navigates the criminal underworld of Gotham in the aftermath of The Batman, rising to power as a ruthless crime lord. With such a premise, The Penguin has many more similarities to The Sopranos than any other comic book project. For one, Oz Cobb and Tony Soprano are both physically imposing main characters who have to manage ruthless crime families.

In fact, Colin Farrell’s prosthetics even make him look physically like Tony Soprano, and his complex relationship with his mother adds a more nuanced similarity. Beyond that, both The Penguin and The Sopranos feature crime families at their center. This means that both deal with well-written relationships and bonds that make viewers unsure of whom to root for, or who will betray whom. Adding in the visual language of a mobster story, The Penguin is more like a modern Sopranos than a Batman spin-off and, as its excellent reception proved, was a true masterpiece.

Although The Penguin's Sopranos comparisons could be used against it as a comic book story, they actually have the opposite effect. In the 2020s, superhero TV shows have become more abundant than ever, with constantly increasing scale, budgets, and connectivity to wider franchises. As a result, this type of superhero show has become somewhat stale, which is what makes The Penguin so special. By embodying a true crime drama like The Sopranos, The Penguin established itself as a standout in the superhero realm.

Beyond a single shot of the Bat-signal in the final minutes of The Penguin's ending, the show has no overt connections to a world filled with superheroes and villains. Yes, there are Easter eggs and references that Batman fans will recognize, but they are presented in a grounded way. Ultimately, The Penguin becomes a crime drama through and through, shaking off any superhero trappings that may have plagued TV shows of the genre in other franchises of late.

All of this makes The Penguin a true masterpiece from beginning to end, but it makes the unclear future of the franchise much harder to take. In 2026, it was confirmed that The Batman - Part II had hit more production hurdles, with Matt Reeves stepping away from the production due to personal issues. Steven Soderbergh was hired to complete production, but, added to the already lengthy delay between the first movie and its sequel, this caused more worries that The Batman - Part III may never happen.

Also in 2026, it was announced that James Gunn and Peter Safran were stepping down as the co-heads of DC Studios, further throwing the future of the franchise into doubt. After all, Gunn was a big advocate of Reeves and his vision for The Batman universe. Now, with Gunn no longer in charge and Reeves continually struggling to balance his personal struggles and the commitment that The Batman requires, the future of this sect of the DC Universe, including The Penguin and its characters, hangs in the balance.

DCU fans are still reeling from the surprise ousting of James Gunn and Peter Safran as the heads of DC Studios, creating more than a few big questions

The final nail in this possible proverbial coffin could be Robert Pattinson's recent casting as James Bond. This could pull the actor away from playing Batman for an extended period of time, further casting a shadow over it. Of course, all could be well for the future of The Batman's Epic Crime Saga, which fans of The Penguin would certainly hope for. Unfortunately, though, the continuation of HBO's modern Sopranos masterpiece is only speculative as of 2026's conclusion.
