#3398. ‘I Play Rocky’ Star P.J. Byrne Isn’t a Scene-Stealer — He’s Something Better

You might not always remember his name, but you know P.J. Byrne. A master of “hey, I love that guy!” roles, the actor is often classified as a scene-stealer, thanks to standout turns in everything from “The Wolf of Wall Street” and “Babylon” to “Coyote vs. Acme” and “The Rainmaker.”

Byrne is funny, yes, but also energetic and an eager scene partner. He improves his projects not by simply showing up and grabbing some quick guffaws, but by really doing the work, learning his characters inside and out, and making it a priority to truly understand his directors. In his own words, he’s not stealing scenes; he’s elevating them. He doesn’t ever want to be the best thing in a film or show — he wants his process to help everything be better. Related Stories ‘Elsinore’ Review: Andrew Scott’s Towering Performance as a Dying Actor Can’t Overcome AIDS-Movie Awards Bait Clichés Jim Cummings Wakes Up to a Post-One-Night-Stand Crisis in ‘DISC’ — Watch the Short

He brings that same approach and ethic to his latest turn as iconic super-producer Irwin Winkler in Peter Farrelly’s crowd-pleasing semi-biopic “I Play Rocky.” Farrelly’s film tracks the “only in Hollywood!” making of Sylvester Stallone’s smash hit “Rocky,” a true underdog story that hinges on the constant rejection of the then-unknown star, who was intent on starring in the film he had written. Stallone’s quest is aided by the support of Winkler and his partner Robert Chartoff (also an excellent Toby Kebbell), who went so far as to mortgage their own homes to make “Rocky” a reality.

Well, it paid off — for both the eventual Best Picture winner “Rocky” and Farrelly’s own film, which also features a massive star turn from Anthony Ippolito as Sly. Sure, there’s lots of drama in the film (Stallone’s physical toll stands out), but Byrne consistently brings his signature good humor and big laughs to Winkler, without ever making the Hollywood icon feel too big or crazy for this particular story.

“For me, it’s actually the most grounded performance I’ve ever had, but — wildly! — getting some of the biggest laughs of my career,” Byrne told IndieWire during a recent interview. That’s the product of a process Byrne has worked on for decades. But as seems to be the case with an actor who is just as gregarious and charming in an interview as you’d expect, it’s also because of the collaborations that really get him excited. That’s better than scene-stealing.

The following interview has been edited and condensed for clarity and length.

IndieWire: You’re the kind of performer that, when you show up in a project, I’m like, “Oh, my God, I’m so excited to see him!” You steal scenes by making them better. You’re not chewing the scenery, you’re not stomping in, but you are adding this extra oomph to everything.

P.J. Byrne: I really believe all ships rise with the tide. If someone hogs the scene, or they want to get all the hits, it just goes south. I’ve just been doing this so long now, and it’s been my 10,000 hours. It started when Mike Nichols saw me and was like, “You need to go do whatever you want” [in “Charlie Wilson’s War”]. That gave me the fearlessness with Marty to make up my own monologue for [“The Wolf of Wall Street”] and just go crazy. I think all these great directors see, “You know what? He does the work.”

Before I start filming anything — and this sounds nuts — I try to show up two weeks before, and I literally just live in a hotel, almost to the point, I’m in my underwear, I’m getting food delivered, and I’m [looking at the script] like, “Where can I raise moments and how can I elevate this character and make this moment truly pop?” It’s not to win it from anyone else. I have to make sure it’s not trite, and it potentially could be zeitgeist-y, and it potentially is a tee-up for everybody else to do it. But I also know, if you’re going to improvise and add stuff, it has to be a nuclear weapon.

I always make the joke, my bio will be, “P.J. Byrne, Over the Shoulder, Out of Focus.” I know when the camera is coming to me. I know I get one shot. It better be a nuclear weapon, because then that gives me the freedom. Directors, like the Mike Nicholses or the Martys or the Damien Chazelles, they’re like, “Just go.” Peter was like, “Get the handcuffs off him. We’ve trust that he’s done the work and passed us knowing that character.” But it’s so important to me to take their vision, because after a while you realize what they really want, and then you can imbue your character perfectly into that and then share that with the other cast members. But that is a lot of work. It’s a crazy amount of work.

You cannot just show up on the day and be like, “Oh, here’s a line that I think that I can really put my signature on.”

Look, some people might have that gift. My gift is coming up with 10 amazing ones, calling friends, “Anything like that, whatever, how’s this one, whatever.” But don’t get me wrong, when the scenes happen, if you get one shot, I have my nuclear weapon. If we’re doing it a couple times, I’ve got four more to throw in the mix, and maybe the fourth wins. But that, to me, is the most fun on set. I’m so crazily prepared. I could still do probably all the lines of the movie now, or some of the [other movies] that I’ve done.

I did a small part in “Green Book,” and really, there are no small parts. I so believe that. Doing these small parts gets me into the world of all these people, and then that grows within that project, or I get a ton of repeat business. But that’s the best interview to ever do. It’s like, see me in action, see how I’m on the set, see what I can bring and try to elevate everybody. I’m never down, like a Friday night at 4:00 a.m., I’m still the Energizer Bunny. That’s a big part of me, because I just know it’s like we’re so lucky to be doing this. Then, I always say, “ABC,” always be classy. It’s so easy to be nice.

I know, it really is. And it makes you feel better. It doesn’t feel good to be a jerk or to be angry or to hold onto things.

It makes no sense to me. But if I see anyone sort of slacking, it makes me crazy, because I’m probably friends with the writer or whoever’s involved. They’ve put years of their lives into this. We don’t need any cancers. This is such a team effort. That’s why this movie in particular was so special, because everybody was there to crush.

The fact that Peter gave me this chance, and Rick Montgomery, I did a commercial with him years ago. They’re always like, “He needs a bigger part in a movie. P.J. needs a bigger shot.” Toby Emmerich, I did “Horrible Bosses” and “Final Destination 5” with him. They all were sort of rooting for me to finally get the shot. And because I had that, I saw it in Anthony. Anthony was getting his shot. It’s about giving Rocky a shot.

This film doesn’t work without you and Toby being an incredibly believable duo. How did you two build that bond?

Me, in this movie, is nothing without Toby. Anything positive is because of that beautiful, insanely good actor, the great Toby Kebbell. There’s so much truth. It’s an interesting thing when you show up at set like, “We have to have a 20-year relationship. I’ve just met you nine minutes ago, and action.” You know when you meet people, you’re like, “Oh, we’re going to be homies. We’re going to be friends forever”? We had a conscious effort of just looking at each other. I think it comes through. We’re having whole conversations just looking at each other, because that’s really what producers are. They don’t talk a lot. They just observe the world.

What did you know about this real story before you came on board?

All I really knew was that he demanded to play the part. I knew that what he was doing in his life, that he had no money. Those are the fundamentals. The crazy part to me is the fact that the studio wanted him to fail. We all know how hard it is to make movies, and when the studio is purposely waiting for you to die, essentially, that was an extraordinary moment. The fact that it turned out this way, with the insane low budget, and they’re doing one takes, and we find the Steadicam, thank God.

Did you know that the real guy showed up when we were doing the steps scene? The man that made that camera, Garrett Brown. When you watch football games and you see the cameras drop, he’s the camera master of making the Steadicam, and everything else. The shot you see in the movie of the girl running up the stairs, that is actual footage, that’s real footage of his wife from 50 years ago. And he’s from “Sesame Street!” It’s like, what a cute place for it to come from.

OK, so this is crazy. Let’s just say, I knew of him, because he produced “The Wolf of Wall Street.” I know the power of Irwin Winkler, because when we were doing scenes, and there’s a thousand people in a room, and it’s just craziness, Irwin Winkler walks on with Marty Scorsese and 1,000 people shut up. You’re just like, “Who’s this? What’s happened?” People are very quiet for Marty, but when those two were chatting on set, it was like 1,000 people are quiet. It’s like, “OK, that’s an interesting asset that this man has.”

When I knew this was coming, I was like, “I have to get a shot at this. I must.” Thank God, Peter and Rick, they’re like, “Put it down. Let’s go. Let’s see what you got, baby.” So then when I did get the part, Irwin said, “Come over to my house, and we’ll chat.” It’s like, “Oh, fuck.” I go over, and he lives in a mansion north of Sunset Boulevard, and he calls it “the house that Rocky built.” It is every magical thing that you can imagine. He’s so gracious, his wife’s lovely.

You go into this amazing old school office, and you’re just, “Can I write every script and take meetings and calls in this room?” What’s so intimidating is, everybody famous from 1960 to present day, there’s a picture of them on his wall with him staring at you while you’re like, “Hi, can I ask about…?” And then he has a film crew there doing a documentary, so they’re filming me asking him questions. It’s an intimidating thing, because he remembers 50 years ago like it’s 15 minutes ago.

I learned from our own interview with Anthony that, while Sly said for a while that he wasn’t involved, he actually met with Peter before the film was made. But Peter was like, “Can you not talk about this? We don’t want you to feel too involved.” And then he went too far to the loop.

Yes. Crazy. Crazy. Crazy. No, yeah, they both blessed it. They both blessed the script. It’s like they blessed us playing those parts separately.

When you are on set with someone like Anthony, who is about to have this massive breakout, what does it feel like for you?

This is super meta, it’s life imitating art. He’s just a kid from Long Island. You’ve got to remember, what is he, 24 when he’s auditioning? We’re shooting, he’s 25. Sylvester was 29, 30, doing this movie. He’s also a younger kid playing this part. He’s number one on the call sheet. This is his first gigantic movie. He’s got Tracy Letts and Matt Dillon, he’s got Peter Farrelly. So it’s very intimidating. This is the greatest part ever, where you have to do the thing of a real thing that happened in a movie.

But the fact that we are living, in the theme of Sylvester Stallone, let’s give somebody a chance, it played out through all of us. I say it all time, I’m so lucky to have been around extraordinary performances, like Leo in “Wolf of Wall Street.” Margot Robbie in “Babylon,” when they do the scene where she comes on the set, and she has to cry, and she does one tear and then two tears, that was real every time. You become an audience member. Even though you’re there and you’re saying your lines, a part of your brain is like, “We’re in the zone, it’s happening.” And that happened with Anthony.

At times, I felt like, “Did Sylvester Stallone travel through space and time and possess a 25-year-old kid’s body?” It’s so natural, and subtle, and soulful, and heartfelt. I would literally look at Peter, and I was like, “He is the greatest actor ever?” It can be an “SNL” performance; it could be a caricature; everybody does a version of him. And it wasn’t just that. It was soulful.

At what point did you realize this was going to become such a crowd-pleaser? I wasn’t at the TIFF premiere, but I went the next morning, and that screening was like being at a Super Bowl or something. Everyone was constantly clapping and cheering and yelling.

None of us thought it would be that. [The TIFF premiere] is the greatest viewing experience of watching a movie that I’m in that I’ve ever had. People are jumping up during the movie, screaming and missing lines because they’re clapping. That was the greatest thing. I was like, “They’ve got to watch it again!” The standing ovation at the end, they stayed up as we were walking on the stage. It was almost an out-of-body experience. It was pure and beautiful. And then, thank God, there were so many moments where I added stuff, but the moment that I didn’t know was going to get that big of a laugh was, you know when the boxing choreographer comes on?

I do. The best boxing choreographer in Hollywood!

That guy’s incredible, too, that guy is so sick. In the original scene, though, I didn’t come on where he gives me his jacket, we added that little thing: “Oh, I’ll take your jacket. … That was interesting.” Also, in that bit, my character, all he said is, “It’s a boxing movie.” I went to Peter, I was like, “There has to be something more, because at this point, he’s never boxed, he can’t box, Stephan [James, who plays Carl Weathers] can’t box.” I’m like, “Let me get the world’s greatest boxing choreographer,” because the job as a producer is to put out fires and lower risk.

I was so nervous about that night because it was the night before Thanksgiving. I know it was late shooting, so I’m like, “Am I going to add a whole bit here at the end of this goddamn thing?” But to Peter’s cred, he’s like, “Well, let’s see what you got.” All those little things that you add, it just shows, if you do the work, if you’re true to what the character is, you’re true to the essence of what the film is, moments like that happen.

If you prepare enough, you can make character choices that are informed. I hear this from a lot of performers: “If you know it enough, you have more freedom.”

But you have to have a director — and this is the big part — who is fearless. Meaning, again, Peter, Chazelle, Marty, Clint Eastwood. They’re just like, “This is what I’m doing. I know what I’m doing, and then I’m going to pass the keys to everybody.” When you have other people who are operating out of fear … they’re not wanting to be creative, everyone’s tight and tense, and you feel it on set, and there’s no room to grow or play. You’re just hitting speed bumps the whole way.

You are also in another movie this year that I love, “Coyote vs. Acme.”

We’re starting to see a push to have it recognized as an animated film, including at the Oscars.

Apparently, they’re technically allowed. It’s over 75 percent animation, so they are allowed to be put into that category.

What does that possibility feel like for you, after everything this film had to go through to even get released?

The director, Dave Green, is a legend. I lived this process with this beautiful human. He’s another one of the kindest, classiest people, the way he handled the whole process, always being calm in the storm. We all knew, and as we’re doing it, something special is happening. We can all feel it. He’s another guy who’s like, “Let P.J. run and [John] Cena go, let Will [Forte] go.” That was another big, important thing, just that this movie is out there.

But also the biggest part truly, in my heart, is Eric Bauza. He just passed away, and he was the nicest, warmest, loveliest human being you’ve ever met. I really believe he’s our generational talent for voiceovers. He is the guy of our moment. He was presenting an award at the 2024 Annie Awards — and the bulk of his income came through Warner Bros., that’s the bulk of this man’s income — and he was the first person, art over commerce, going, “Release ‘Coyote vs. Acme!’” Against the people that pay him!

Please, God, let this movie be nominated. The work, the music, the animation, there’s so many extraordinary things. To think that that was not going to see the light of day! The fact that the world loved it, it’s got 96 percent on Rotten Tomatoes. It’s just like, the world’s right. Every once in a while, the world is right.

Do you get recognized on the street? And if so, what do you get recognized for?

It’s like anything and everything. Sometimes, they’ll just be like, “You’re a great stand-up comic.” I’m like, “I don’t even know what that means. I’ve never done that before.” Sometimes people hear my voice, and they’re like, “Are you from that cartoon?” That stuff, God, it goes back years, too. I did a show 15 years ago called “The Game,” and if I’m in Atlanta, they’re like, “Let’s go. I hate you, but I love you!” People screaming at me. Sometimes it’s “Wolf.” Sometimes super cinephiles go crazy for “Babylon.” They go absolutely nuts, corner you. Anybody talking about me? I’m always happy. That means I’m working or doing something.

My last question is my favorite to ask of people who I feel like have already done so many different things: What have you not done yet that you really want to do?

God, I would love to do a “Hoosiers” and be a coach. No one’s putting me in a war movie, but if you look at it now, I’m kind of growing into the general role, or some higher officer role. I want to be a bad guy in “Star Wars.” I want to be like, “Let me see how someone spends $340 million.” I want to be the man in “Mission: Impossible” standing next to Tom Cruise, or being the other guy on a computer. All of the big massive movies, because I miss doing that stuff, and they don’t shoot in LA as much, those big monster, masterful movies.

Ultimately, I want to work with great directors who are fearless. That’s the real thing. The directors that go, “P.J., take the handcuffs off and go out there and play, let them throw the touchdown pass to you.” The quarterback’s the star, but I promise I will make a great play as the wide receiver. Whoever that person is, whoever’s doing that, I will show up, and I promise I will score for you.

#3397. Paramount+ Just Made Its Biggest Mistake With Its Surging 99-Minute Fantasy Movie

Amanda M. Castro is a Network TV writer at Collider and a New York–based journalist whose work has appeared in Newsweek, where she is an Associate Editor, and The U.S. Sun, where she previously served as a Senior Consumer Reporter.

She specializes in network television coverage, delivering sharp, thoughtful analysis of long-running procedural hits and ambitious new dramas across broadcast TV. At Collider, Amanda explores character arcs, storytelling trends, and the cultural impact of network series that keep audiences tuning in week after week.

Born and raised in Puerto Rico, Amanda is bilingual and holds a degree in Communication, Film, and Media Studies from the University of New Haven.

Avatar Aang: The Last Airbender has a lot of great things about it. Avatar fans have waited so long to see Aang, Katara, Sokka, Toph, and Zuko as grown-ups, and the movie's visual effects leave you in awe. At times, you realize the possibilities this franchise has beyond the original TV series. At the same time, Avatar Aang reminds you that the story could have played out differently if we'd watched the TV show instead of the film.

Set almost a decade after the Hundred Year War, the story follows Team Avatar as they take on the responsibilities of adulthood. Aang still faces the challenge of surviving as an Air Nomad when he gets into another mess after stealing an ancient relic and meeting the ancient airbender. It introduces new Avatar lore, a villain with complicated motivations, spiritual mythology, and a chance to explore how the world has changed since the gang defeated Ozai. Somehow, all of that has to fit into one movie, and it shows. Avatar: Seven Havens reminds us that this franchise is at its best when it has room to develop its characters and let its stories unfold. Avatar Aang could have used the same courtesy.

One of the biggest draws of this movie is seeing what happened to the Gaang after the war. They’re no longer kids traveling the world together. Sokka helps rebuild the Southern Water Tribe, Toph teaches metalbending, Katara has responsibilities in Republic City, and Zuko runs the Fire Nation. They have their own lives now, which is precisely what makes reuniting them so interesting, except the movie doesn’t do nearly enough with it.

Katara, Sokka, Toph, and Zuko are so caught up in Aang’s story that we rarely see how adulthood has changed them or what has become of their relationships. While the movie offers some clues about the dynamics fans may want to see, it doesn't give them enough time to unfold before yet another conflict, revelation, or plot twist. It is really disappointing that the original series created such a wonderful image of the characters as good friends in each other’s lives. They quarreled, made each other's lives difficult, and occasionally had absolutely nothing to do with saving the world. Not every word in a film should advance the plot; sometimes it's just about spending time together.

In this film, Team Avatar is back, yet it seems determined not to let us spend time with them. Fans didn't need another world-ending evil to excuse their reunion; we just wanted to see the characters get to know each other again, joke about their journey, or figure out the outcomes of their lives.

Allison King’s Avatar Aang: The Last Airbender: A Novel adds new scenes, perspectives, and storylines that weren’t included in the movie. It includes villain POV chapters, additional material involving Suki, conversations between Team Avatar, and more attention to Aang’s memories of the Air Nomads. It’s the sort of expansion that makes you wonder what the movie might have looked like with another few hours to work with.

To be clear, the novelization isn’t some miraculous improvement on the film. Expanding a story doesn’t automatically improve its characterization, and some of the book’s character dynamics and relationships don’t particularly work for me, but it does highlight how much more there was to explore. For example, Aang’s grief isn't new —the original series already showed how much losing his people hurt him, and the film explores that struggle again as he grapples with saving Air Nomad culture. However, understanding grief and seeing a character deal with it are two different matters. The novel gives room to revisit his memories, explore his fears, and reflect on moments the film rushes.

The same goes for everyone else. Toph’s personal life, Katara’s responsibilities, Sokka’s work rebuilding his home, and Zuko’s transition into leadership could have been meaningful subplots instead of background information. The novel doesn’t necessarily get all those characters right (especially some points about Toph), but the extra material makes it painfully obvious that this story wasn't running out of things to say.

The art book offers a different angle on the film's potential. Avatar: The Last Airbender: The Art of the Movie shows how character designs, locations, hybrid animals, and animation methods contributed to the filmmaking process. One of the film's best parts is the combination of 2D characters with a CG environment, and the book makes it easier for viewers to appreciate the work done behind the camera.

Even the returning characters’ designs have a story to share. Zuko’s design went through several variations before the animators settled on a look that matched the Fire Lord's image. The artists faced the challenge of showing how the characters evolved and representing that evolution visually while staying true to the original characters.

That’s the kind of detail the movie should have had time to appreciate itself. The world has changed, the characters have changed; there are new locations, new creatures, new political tensions, and a history that stretches far beyond the original series. Yet the movie is so busy getting through its story that some of its most interesting ideas never get the attention they deserve.

The success some movies achieve with different audiences is undeniable. The original series used its three seasons to build a unique world and develop the characters, leading to the exciting journey that culminated in the ultimate victory over Ozai. Importantly, the movie could afford long pauses, while the series’ best episodes focused on events with little relation to the main plot; that is what made them successful.

Avatar: Seven Havens, which has already secured a second season, continues that tradition. A serialized story has the luxury of developing its mythology over time, introducing conflicts without immediately resolving them, and giving its characters room to surprise us. That’s particularly valuable in a franchise where the world itself is just as interesting as the Avatar’s central mission.

It would have been nice to see Avatar Aang take this route. We need an episode where Aang goes back to the Air Temples while Zuko deals with all the matters that come with being the Fire Lord. Toph can live a life outside metalbending sessions and drooling over Tagah. Katara and Sokka can be siblings instead of just members of a group assembled to tackle yet another danger.

The film features great animation and a delightful reunion between the heroes, but that doesn’t substitute for good storytelling. Avatar Aang is full of enough ideas for an entire season, and it is sad to see them crammed into a single motion picture. Avatar has all the time in the world; it can take its time, and the world will wait.

#3394. Christopher Nolan and Guillermo del Toro Break Down ‘The Odyssey’ Monsters and AI’s Limitations with Production VFX Supervisor Andrew Jackson

With “The Odyssey,” Christopher Nolan ventured into the realm of fantasy for the first time, realizing a time of towering monsters, swirling whirlpools, and apparent magic. The production is a true showcase for his longtime collaborator, production visual effects supervisor Andrew Jackson, who began working on the film‘s elaborate set pieces far ahead of production.

“What’s essential is having the visual effects team be part of the main unit through prep, through the shoot, everything — and not treating you guys as somebody that’s going to come on afterwards and add to the film,” Nolan said, speaking with Jackson during a panel following a Visual Effects Society screening of “The Odyssey” at the IMAX auditorium of AMC Theatres’ Universal Cinema location in Los Angeles. The discussion was moderated by Guillermo del Toro. Related Stories ‘I Play Rocky’ Star P.J. Byrne Isn’t a Scene-Stealer — He’s Something Better ‘Elsinore’ Review: Andrew Scott’s Towering Performance as a Dying Actor Can’t Overcome AIDS-Movie Awards Bait Clichés

“What I’ve found through the years is to treat the effects as a remedial thing that is separate from everything is a big mistake,” del Toro added. “The beauty of it and the respect for the crafts is to integrate them early enough so that they are part of a physical solution as well as the post-production solution.”

The panel offered a detailed breakdown of several standout sequences in “The Odyssey,” including the early encounter with the Cyclops, which was realized with a mix of animatronic puppetry, digital effects, and a performance by clowning veteran Bill Irwin. Nolan shared that Jackson, who started as a model maker, is always one of his earliest collaborators — he was the first person to read the script for “Oppenheimer,” even. Integrating the various design elements of the Cyclops required a constant conversation from pre-production through the editing room.

“We were forced to shorten the time we had to build it,” Jackson began. Nolan then offered a joke: “I like the word forced. It’s good. I’m getting used to my crew members just vilifying me completely as we sit in these Q&As.”

“We both know that the result of being forced to trim away all the more complex parts of the plan resulted in a solution that was better than it would’ve been if we had continued with the original plan,” Jackson continued. “We basically just made a very, very simple marionette, which had still detailed solid components for the physical body, but just missed out on all the complicated joints and where the parts intersected. But the fact that it was simple and moved in a fascinating way that had a life of its own became really compelling.”

“I knew that one day you’d be sitting here and Guillermo del Toro would say it was perfectly integrated, so it’s all worth it,” Nolan said.

As with many industry Q&As these days, the topic of artificial intelligence’s impact on the filmmaking process, particularly on the field of visual effects, was addressed. Nolan, Jackson, and del Toro each emphasized the need for human oversight of the technology’s implementation, suggesting that “The Odyssey” could not have been realized without the conversations that happened across the film’s various departments.

“In an age with artificial intelligence looming — with synthetic creativity around us, or whatever — it’s actually very important to acknowledge the artistry that goes into the compositing process,” Nolan said. “My demand on the compositors and the animators is always to be using their eye rather than their brain, if you like, rather than simulating things or creating a simulation reality. I want them to look at it with an artist’s eye: the way matte painters who were working on glass paintings did, so that there’s an impressionistic quality in the composites.”

“The defense of the human touch and the defense of the craft is as urgent, if not more urgent, to VFX because it is the one that has gotten assailed the fastest by things like AI, which was not invented or demanded from any artist,” del Toro said. “It was demanded and created by people that were alien to that and appeal only to time and money mostly.”

“Well, time and money and also a misunderstanding of the process,” Nolan said.

“You’re absolutely going to need artists to know even whether the new tools have delivered things that you want. You need people to be able to assess that,” Jackson said.

#3392. Stephen King's 8-Episode Sci-Fi Masterpiece Delivers A 10/10 Time Travel Story

It is hard for sci-fi writers to get time travel right, thanks to its many contradictions and paradoxes, but one Stephen King adaptation released by Hulu in 2016 managed this feat. There is a reason that Rick and Morty’s titular scientific super genius had a strict “No Time Travel” rule when it came to the anarchic show’s weekly animated misadventures. Even in a comedic context, fictional time travel is always tough to follow and tougher to explain.

Where a dystopian sci-fi show like Station Eleven can flash back and forth between before and after the end of the world with panache, any story where the main characters themselves travel through time opens itself up to all manner of tricky questions. Many great screen depictions of sci-fi, like Netflix’s three-season masterpiece Dark, have constructed elaborate systems to keep track of intersecting realities and overlapping timelines.

However, horror legend and Pennywise creator Stephen King made this achievement look easy with one 2016 adaptation. Based on the author’s 2011 novel of the same name, 11.22.63 sees the English teacher Jake Epping use his friend Al Templeton’s experimental time travel machine to return to 1960 in the hopes of preventing John F. Kennedy’s infamous assassination on the titular fateful date.

This sounds like a fairly straightforward plot, but, like any time travel story, 11.22.63 inevitably introduces some twists and turns into the plan. Primarily, Epping discovers that he has become unexpectedly attached to his new life in the swinging ‘60s, and he is subsequently unsure whether he wants to go through with the plan since it will mean returning to his own present-day reality.

Disgraced actor James Franco plays Epping, while American Beauty supporting star Chris Cooper plays his conflicted friend Templeton. The uncertainty that 11.22.63’s protagonists face is complicated by characters like Lucy Fry’s Marina Oswald, George MacKay’s Bill Turcotte, and Daniel Webber’s Lee Harvey Oswald but, fortunately, this is the only part of 11.22.63’s story that feels uncertain and complicated.

Although he is best known as a legendary horror author thanks to hit books like Carrie, It, and The Shining, King also penned the iconic fantasy saga The Dark Tower and has written many crime, mystery, and thriller novels in his time. In 11.22.63’s elegant time travel story, the writer proves he is also a master of this infamously tricky sci-fi subgenre, too. 11.22.63’s handling of time travel finds a perfect balance between intricacy and simplicity.

Often, time travel stories either become extremely convoluted and technical, as seen in director Shane Carruth’s infamously complex indie movie Primer, or extremely simplistic and cavalier. This approach is exemplified by the Back to the Future trilogy, a set of movies that offer viewers a ripping good story that makes absolutely no sense in terms of its in-universe time travel mechanics.

11.22.63 finds a perfect balance between these two extremes, with a fictional take on time travel that feels rooted in recognizable reality, but never becomes complicated enough to overshadow the story’s emotional core. The show’s success emboldened HBOMax’s later hit King adaptation It: Welcome to Derry to add a time travel twist to Pennywise’s story in its season 1 finale, a clever addition that made the shared universe of King’s stories feel more immersive and lived-in than ever before.

It is always risky for a creator to establish a shared universe containing many of their works and characters, and it is even riskier when some of the stories in this universe bring time travel into the mix. However, Hulu’s confident adaptation of 11.22.63 proved that, despite being best known as a horror maestro, King can be trusted with sci-fi’s most infamously slippery trope.

Hey, did you see the post-credit scenes in VisionQuest? Of course you did. Did you see the eight pre-credit installments, aka VisionQuest's actual episodes? The 421 million minutes streamed over one week would suggest that you certainly did. Now, be honest: are you talking to any of your fellow MCU fans about the series itself? Or are you talking about the Doctor Doom/Scarlet Witch post credit scene, and what it means for the upcoming Avengers: Doomsday? If you said the former, you either clearly missed the "be honest" part of the question, or your pants are on fire. That post-credit scene is the only thing anyone wants to talk about, and that's a problem. So, at the risk of being labeled a heretic for even suggesting it, here goes: Marvel, the post-credit scenes have to go.

It didn't have to come to this. It all began innocently enough with the stinger that came at the end of 2008's Iron Man, where S.H.I.E.L.D. director Nick Fury (Samuel L. Jackson) told Tony Stark (Robert Downey Jr.) he was "putting together a team." If that didn't pop your bottle, shop your K-mart, or blossom your bloomers, then you had no soul. It was a brilliant, touchstone moment that foreshadowed something truly special.

And it only got better from there. Agent Coulson (Clark Gregg) finding Thor's hammer in Iron Man 2. Captain America (Chris Evans) waking up in the present in Captain America: The First Avenger. The introduction of the imposing Thanos — Than-freakin'-os (Josh Brolin), for crying out loud — in The Avengers. And who could forget the collective, worldwide "awwww" upon seeing Dancing Baby Groot in Guardians of the Galaxy. Scenes that either teased what was to come, or were simply there to entertain; it didn't really matter. They were good, sometimes very good, and became must-see moments.

Then, somewhere along the way, they began to suck. Hard. Ant-Man & The Wasp: Quantumania introduced a threat in Jonathan Majors' Kang that, even if it had come to fruition, had the feel of "been there, done that" with Thanos. Films like Eternals and Thor: Love and Thunder introduced characters — Starfox (Harry Styles) and Hercules (Brett Goldstein), respectively — who have never reappeared. It's like someone realized that the movie didn't have an end-credit scene yet, so they said, "Hey, let's come up with something, even if it never goes anywhere." The MCU had created its own monster, and now had to feed it. Worse, the expectations for post-credit scenes expanded to films that weren't even in the MCU, prompting websites that specifically address whether there are after-credit scenes or not. Let me save you the bother: Titanic does not have an after-credits scene.

Then they re-released Avengers: Endgame with four additional scenes. If you paid for "Infinity Vision," that is. Common folk who saw it in "Normal Vision" got screwed out of one scene, which arguably wasn't even worth the extra $8 to see. In fact, none of them were truly must-see, but you had to see them, because, dammit, it might be important to know for Avengers: Doomsday. Guess what? It'll all be disclosed in Avengers: Doomsday, so you paid money to find out something you were going to find out anyway.

And then came VisionQuest and its two post-credit scenes. One has Ultron (James Spader) holding Jocasta's flash drive, which likely falls into the Starfox/Hercules camp of something that will never come up again. Another has Doctor Doom lifting rocks off of Scarlet Witch after the events of Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness and awaking her. At least, we assume it's her. She looks as much like Elizabeth Olsen as the Scorpion King looked like Dwayne "The Rock" Johnson in The Mummy Returns (hint: he doesn't). With one scene that likely means nothing, and another that at least appears to have not even bothered including Olsen whatsoever, overshadowing a very good series in VisionQuest by changing the conversation, the post-credit scenes have crossed the line.

What is the point in having a post-credit scene you throw together, if it's going to negate the work you put into the series leading into it? Here's an idea: have a series and/or movie that is just post-credit scenes, and put the movie proper after it. "Sure, the post-credit scenes were good, but did you see the post-post-credit movie after it? Dude, it's epic!"

And now, they're re-releasing Spider-Man: Brand New Day on December 4th with "a few surprises that weren't in the original cut." What are those few surprises? It's hard not to believe there isn't at least one additional post-credit scene that ties into Avengers: Doomsday, at least if you see it in "Infinity Vision." Otherwise, you have to wait two weeks. Two measly weeks. Enough already. If there isn't any artistic merit to adding a post-credit scene — and forgive the cynicism, but it smells like "cash grab" — then don't bother.

#3389. David Ellison on Elon Musk’s Skydance Investment, Trump and ‘Rush Hour 4,’ and Whether He Would’ve Made ‘Digger’

Though David Ellison has been around Hollywood for a while now, he’s undoubtedly our newest media mogul and still a fresh face when it comes to being the center stage headliner at fill-in-the-blank business media conference. There’s still a lot we don’t know about him and a lot of questions people have about his plans for Skydance, his politics, and his taste in movies.

So on Wednesday when he spoke with Andrew Ross Sorkin of the New York Times at the DealBook Summit on Wednesday, he had a chance to get candid about a whole range of subjects. It’s early days at Skydance, with changes to the C-suite coming daily, so he’s still keeping his cards a little close to his sport jacket. But we did learn a few things about what he envisions for Skydance. Related Stories Christopher Nolan and Guillermo del Toro Break Down ‘The Odyssey’ Monsters and AI’s Limitations with Production VFX Supervisor Andrew Jackson ‘I Play Rocky’ Star P.J. Byrne Isn’t a Scene-Stealer — He’s Something Better

“One of our guiding thematics has always been where entertainment is heading,” Ellison said. “It’s that great Gretsky quote, skate to where the puck is going, not to where the puck has been, and that’s been what’s guided the company.”

Following a report that the world’s richest man had invested $1 billion into Ellison’s Skydance, leading many to think there’s some bigger picture brewing between Skydance and Starlink, Ellison did confirm that Musk is an investor and shareholder, and though he couldn’t comment on anything on which they may be collaborating, he’s welcoming the opportunity.

“He’s the greatest entrepreneur of all time,” Ellison said. “He doesn’t invest in a lot of companies, so to have his vote of confidence and to have him as a shareholder is an honor and a privilege, and if there’s ever an opportunity to collaborate in the future, from our perspective it would be a privilege.”

Sorkin did double back and ask if Ellison will still allow Alex Gibney’s “Musk” documentary to air on HBO as been planned. He said that HBO has a Pay-1 deal with A24, so of course they would honor that agreement, and they “believe in independence and we don’t believe in censorship of any kind.”

One problem: A24 didn’t produce “Musk” as Ellison said. It’s a Bleecker Street film. So we’ll put a little asterisk on that answer.

Tom Cruise’s mega flop “Digger” has the ironic and unfortunate distinction of being the final movie released by Warner Bros. Discovery. And Ellison was asked “how risky” he would continue to be in the context of how much money “Digger” stands to lose. Ellison started by saying that Cruise is “one of the seminal artists of our time,” that Skydance has made eight movies previously with him, and they’re making a “Days of Thunder” sequel before (hopefully) heading into making “Top Gun 3.”

Ellison then described a long story that involved sleeping on Hans Zimmer’s couch before landing on the age old, “what’s the budget?”

“I spent the last 16 years of my life on the filmmaking side of this business. I have lived on set, I have slept on Hans Zimmer’s couch, I have been in editorial rooms for 20 hours non-stop, I do understand the creative process of this business,” Ellison said. “The goal has to be in any film that you make is how do you reach the broadest possible audience for that particular story? There is no one size fits all approach. We will make franchise movies, we will make original stories, we will make genre pictures, we will tell stories aimed at audiences from every single walk of life. What is important is that you size the budget to the potential addressable audience.”

Sorkin pushed Ellison hard about what his politics are and who he voted for in the most recent election. He still did not get an answer, but he would not let slide some of the reports that President Trump himself asked about Paramount requesting that the studio make “Rush Hour 4.”

“We are working with Brett [Ratner] on ‘Rush Hour 4,’ which is a sequel to an incredibly successful franchise,” Ellison confirmed. However, he said the first time he heard about the prospect of that movie was when film chief Josh Goldstine walked into his office and mentioned it, not that it came from Trump, and that “there’s a lot of made up stories” out there.

“Rush Hour” director Ratner as a reminder was in 2017 accused of sexual harassment and misconduct by six women as part of a Los Angeles Times report, including actresses Olivia Munn and Natasha Henstridge, claims that he denied. His most recent project was this year’s “Melania” documentary that was released by Amazon MGM.

One thing Ellison has been working with President Trump on is his desire to get passed a federal tax rebate for film productions in the U.S., and he told Sorkin his goal is to see the rebate passed by the end of this year, at which point the new Congress comes into office and a bill has to be reintroduced. He said he had three meetings with the late Senator Lindsay Graham about the problems of film production leaving the country.

Ellison was staunch in pushing back on some data from the Tax Policy Center as shared by Sorkin that while subsidies do influence where productions choose to shoot, it’s not the same as creating measurable economic growth and that it just pulls workers away from other jobs and tourism.

“Categorically that’s just not true. When you actually look at the rebate in the United Kingdom, it has been a boom to their economy, same is true in Canada, same is true in Australia. All those other countries have those rebates because it pencils out,” Ellison said. “If you look at Texas, Paramount was a part of building a 31 percent rebate for all of Taylor Sheridan’s productions. We had a meeting down there with the deputy governor that said, based on their own independent audit, for every dollar that was invested by the state returned $4.70.”

He also stressed that it’s a misnomer that Tom Cruise is the one getting a tax break but that really it goes to helping union, working class film professionals who benefit.

“You are creating jobs, you are helping small businesses, and every other country that has done this in the past has done this because it is economically sustainable,” he added.

Ellison on numerous occasions in earnings calls and in other appearances has expressed his fondness for artificial intelligence and how he feels it’s going to transform Hollywood. He elaborated on that view a little more on Wednesday, calling it not just a tool for artists but a “creative unlock.”

“Going back to the days of Pixar, the lesson was always be wrong as fast as possible…we’re going to be living in a world where you can make the movie not 10 times but 20 times before it gets put out,” Ellison said. “We’re also living in a world where a $750K movie made $500 million because the cost of production has boxed out new voices.”

He’s referring to “Obsession” there, but he also gave the example of the original “Terminator,” which Ellison said James Cameron made for $4 million but today would cost $70 million. He felt the AI tools would help people to make those original stories, and he’s fully on board.

“The relationship we basically have with talent, our understanding of technology and how those two things are fused together, it’s a feedback loop,” Ellison said. “It is the art challenges the technology, technology inspires the art feedback loop. That is what is necessary to meet this moment in time and build the entertainment company of the future.”

#3387. Microsoft Officially Apologized for Yesterday's Outages

If you were having trouble accessing certain services like Microsoft Teams or Outlook, you were not alone. Early Thursday afternoon, many of Microsoft's biggest apps and services were experiencing downtime. According to Downdetector, which tracks user reports of issues with websites and platforms, Microsoft 365, Teams, Copilot, Teams, and OneDrive were all experiencing issues. As of Friday afternoon, Microsoft has restored service to many users, and has officially apologized for the outages.

When I first published this article on Thursday, I couldn't even load Microsoft 365's status page. (I've reported on many service outages, but I can't recall a time when a service's status page was also down.) Even as of Friday afternoon, the page still says "Service degradation on Microsoft 365 (Business or Enterprise)," and Microsoft says the following services may be affected: Exchange Online, Microsoft 365 admin center, Microsoft 365 apps, Microsoft 365 Apps Admin Center, Microsoft 365 Education, Microsoft Copilot 365, Microsoft Defender for Office 365, Microsoft Defender XDR, Microsoft Fabric, Microsoft Graph, Microsoft Intune, Microsoft Planner, Microsoft Power Apps, Microsoft Purview, Microsoft Teams, Microsoft To Do, Power BI, SharePoint Online, Universal Print, and Windows 365.

Looking specifically at Outlook, Microsoft's email service had hundreds of thousands of user reports Thursday afternoon, signaling a major issue somewhere in Microsoft's pipeline. The reports did "slow down" throughout the day, but Downdetector still showed over 50,000 reports coming in every 15 minutes when I checked Thursday afternoon.

While the root cause of the issue was a mystery throughout Thursday's outage, Microsoft confirmed the problem in an apology on Friday. According to the company, "This was a technical issue not related to cyber or AI [or] agents. The incident was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change. We have addressed the underlying issue and continue to restore service to remaining customers and regions."

Microsoft says it is "deeply sorry" for the disruption to its customers and partners. The company says the fix rolled out slower than some might expect, since it wanted to restore service gradually to evaluate stability at each stage. It also says it will release a full post-incident report once it completes a review.

During the outage, the company had confirmed that some of its infrastructure was experiencing elevated load, which it said was likely contributing to the issues. Microsoft then said it was pausing all deployments and moving traffic from affected infrastructure, and that it found that a number of its servers were unexpectedly unavailable after failing health checks. The company then thought a specific component responsible for processing server health may be the reason the system is failing health checks. Microsoft said an alternative service health check method successfully restarted some of the affected servers. The company was then actively restarting and validating affected servers to bring them back to service.

#3386. Wheel Of Time: The Last Battle Officially Releasing June 2027

Robert Jordan's Wheel of Time culminates in one of the greatest showdowns between good and evil in all fantasy, but unfortunately, many people have never actually seen how The Last Battle plays out. Aside from there never being a proper live-action adaptation after the Amazon series' cancellation, there's actually a huge portion of readers that stall out due to fatigue in the middle of the series that's famously become known as "The Slog."

It's a shame, considering how spectacularly the series brings together its countless interconnected storylines, uniting an enormous cast of beloved characters for a truly unforgettable conclusion. The Last Battle, also known as Tarmon Gai'don, is the culmination of everything Jordan spent decades building toward, and it's an event that deserves to be experienced by fans beyond the original books.

Thankfully, that's finally about to become a reality, with an official new adaptation of The Last Battle set to arrive in 2027, offering fans an entirely new way to experience the legendary showdown.

War of the Dragon: The Wheel of Time is an upcoming grand strategy board game from Dire Wolf, the publisher behind Dune: Imperium and Clank!, that will finally give fans the story's finale in an entirely new way. It's also the first official board game adaptation of Robert Jordan's legendary fantasy series, and the project has attracted an enormous amount of attention after its wildly successful Kickstarter campaign.

Unlike traditional adaptations, War of the Dragon puts players directly in control of the conflict between the Light and the Shadow, allowing them to determine how the war unfolds. Players can take control of either side, assembling powerful allies, capturing territories, and preparing for the ultimate confrontation between Rand al'Thor's forces and the Dark One.

The game features two distinct modes, with Hero Mode offering a more accessible experience focused on building alliances and controlling the map. However, it's Epic Mode that fans are really stoked about as it will actually bring Jordan's sprawling fantasy saga to life, complete with massive armies and conflicts, character progression, and story-driven events.

Epic Mode begins with a prologue battle and spans four chapters before culminating in The Last Battle itself. Players commanding the Light can develop iconic characters like Rand, Mat, Perrin, Egwene, and Nynaeve, while those controlling the Shadow can unleash the Forsaken and strengthen the Dark One's forces.

Eventually, everything comes together in an enormous final confrontation, where players deploy the armies and characters they've assembled throughout the campaign. The decisions made along the way directly influence the outcome, so fans can actually experience an alternate version of The Last Battle where the Shadow emerges victorious.

War of the Dragon was massively successful with its crowdfunding campaign, raising over $1.16 million from more than 6,100 Kickstarter backers, absolutely demolishing its original $50,000 goal. The game is currently expected to begin reaching US Kickstarter supporters in the first half of 2027, with international fulfillment following afterward. A retail release is also planned for 2027.

While it certainly isn't a live-action adaptation, War of the Dragon offers something arguably just as exciting, which is the opportunity to rewrite the fate of the entire Wheel of Time universe themselves.

#3385. NFL Condemns Mike Florio's Hitler Joke About Patriots Coach Mike Vrabel

The NFL isn't laughing at Mike Florio's Hitler joke about Mike Vrabel ... blasting the NBC Sports analyst over his crack about the New England Patriots coach's mustache.

According to the New York Post, NFL executive Jeff Miller condemned the remarks, saying the league found them "inappropriate and offensive."

And the NFL apparently isn't letting it slide ... with a league source telling the outlet officials took their concerns directly to NBC Sports, the league's longtime broadcast partner.

As TMZ previously reported, Florio made the eyebrow-raising joke during Tuesday's "PFT Live" while discussing Vrabel's appearance with cohost Chris Simms following New England's game against the Detroit Lions in Munich, Germany.

Simms brought up Vrabel's "German mustache" ... prompting Florio to warn the coach about trimming the sides of his facial hair while in Germany, an apparent reference to Adolf Hitler.

When producer Gary Carter groaned at the joke, Florio doubled down ... declaring, "It's funny, Gary. It was 80 years ago" ... before adding, "Let us have some fun, for crying out loud."

Florio -- who founded Pro Football Talk and has become a familiar face on NBC's NFL coverage -- never mentioned Hitler by name ... though the reference was hard to miss.

As for Vrabel, the Patriots coach had been clean-shaven in previous seasons ... making his newer mustache a noticeable change in appearance.

New England lost Sunday's game to Detroit 35-10, and lost QB Drake Maye to injury ... but it's Florio who's now taking heat off the field.

#3384. 10 Books Like ‘A Court of Thorns and Roses’ You Should Read Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Sarah J. Maas’ lush, romance-soaked series A Court of Thorns and Roses has blossomed into a sprawling, complex fantasy series with millions of dedicated fans, and with good reason. A complex heroine who keeps discovering new depths in herself, fascinating supporting characters who shift from antihero to antivillain in unexpected ways, creative and beautifully rendered world-building—the series has it all, while also being unapologetically romantic (and steamy).

The story of a huntress who is kidnapped by a fae prince and brought to the Spring Court as a prisoner, only to become a key player in all that fae drama, ACOTAR is special, but Maas can only write so fast. If you need more books with the same lush feel, here are 10 to get you started.

It’s no shock that one of Sarah J. Maas’ other series would be recommended for fans of A Court of Thorns and Roses, but there’s a specific reason you should jump into her Crescent City series, especially the third book, House of Flame and Shadow. The most recent ACOTAR book, A Court of Splintered Harmony, revealed that the events of House of Flame and Shadow tie directly into the events in Splintered Harmony, particularly with regard to the character of Feyre’s sister, Nesta. In other words, if you read Splintered Harmony and wondered why Nesta was being so weird, there’s a whole other book series you should dig into immediately.

If Feyre’s grit and determination are your favorite aspect of ACOTAR, Julie Kagawa’s Iron Fey series (starting with The Iron King) will be your next obsession. Meghan Chase has never felt ‘normal’ in her life, and she’s been haunted by her father’s disappearance since she was a child. When her brother also vanishes, she goes on a quest for answers, learns that she’s actually the daughter of a faerie king, and finds herself in a magical world that blurs in elements of Shakespeare’s A Midsummer Night’s Dream. Meghan is determined to save her brother (and herself), but a certain ice-cold fae prince captures her attention, even though he’s as dangerous as he is beautiful.

If you’re looking for some serious romance in your fantasy, Jennifer L. Armentrout’s A Blood and Ash series is a must. Poppy was chosen at birth to be the kingdom’s Maiden, isolated and untouched in order to be ready for her Ascension to ensure the land is protected from the evil force that took her family. But it’s a lonely existence—until Hawke is assigned as her sworn protector. Golden-eyed and beautiful, Hawke offers Poppy the connection she’s craved. When chaos erupts around her, Hawke takes the opportunity to spirit Poppy away. But Hawke has a secret, and Poppy is soon in danger of losing both her heart and the favor of the gods themselves.

If you love how A Court of Thorns and Roses takes the “enemies-to-lovers” trope and builds it into a deep, complex mesh of emotions and plot twists, you’ll love Shelby Mahurin’s Serpent & Dove series. When witch Louise le Blanc flees her coven, she takes shelter in the city of Cesarine, where magic is forbidden, and witches are unceremoniously hunted and burned. Louise’s life gets infinitely more complicated, dangerous, and steamy when she’s trapped into an unwanted marriage with Reid Diggory—who happens to be a huntsman of the Church, charged with tracking down and eliminating witches. And then Louise starts to realize that Reid is actually pretty darn hot.

If you’re looking for a romantasy that’s broadly similar to ACOTAR while being its own thing, read A.K. Mulford’s The Five Crowns of Okrith series, starting with The High Mountain Court. Remy is a red witch, which means she’s in hiding and ready to make a run for it if the fae get near. So when a group of fae shows up at her tavern, she makes for the exit—only to be captured by Prince Hale of the Eastern Court. Instead of striking her down, however, Hale asks Remy for help—he needs to locate two ancient magical artifacts created by red witches, and he needs her red magic to find them. Hale promises to set her free and even reunite her with the red witches still living. More importantly, Remy finds Hale irresistible and has a primal urge to stay with him, no matter what the cost.

Looking for a romantasy with a slightly different vibe from ACOTAR? Variety is the spice of life, after all—and The Fourth Wing delivers. Rebecca Yarros’ Empyrean Series made a huge splash when it debuted, and for good reason—it has everything, from a capable, intelligent heroine thrust into a dangerous scenario (in this case, a dragon rider academy where failure can be deadly) and forced to navigate alliances, conspiracies, and her own heart, which is pushing her towards a romance that might be as dangerous as the dragons themselves.

Love the moral complexity of ACOTAR, where everyone has at least a touch of darkness? Check out The Folk of the Air series by Holly Black. When Jude was a child, the father of her half-sister, the faerie Madoc, murdered her parents and took her back to the Faerie world with him. Raised as part of the gentry, Jude lives in a world where her mortal nature is hated and despised, but she battles for her place at court anyway while struggling with her love-hate relationship with her adoptive father and a growing bond with the titular prince, a relationship that is strictly forbidden. Jude is a fierce and extremely morally gray character, and one that fans of Feyre will adore.

Looking for more smart women at the center of beautifully-rendered fantasy stories? You’ll love Princess Lucero-Elisa de Riqueza of Orovalle, star of this series-starter by Rae Carson. Elisa was chosen for “Service” as a baby, when a godstone was placed in her navel by the gods, signaling that she was destined for greatness. But as a young woman, Elisa is self-hating and miserable. She’s never done anything even remotely great, and spends her time isolated, overweight, and reading military strategy books. One day she’s shocked to discover she’s been married off to the king of a distant land on the brink of war—and suddenly all that rage and book learning becomes invaluable as she struggles to survive an unfamiliar court and help her new homeland survive a dangerous onslaught.

If you loved Feyre’s journey as she discovered unknown reservoirs of power and courage inside herself, you should read Leigh Bardugo’s Grishaverse novels, starting with Shadow and Bone. As a child, Alina was tested by the Grisha and found to possess no magical ability. As an adult, she serves as a cartographer in the army. Charged with guiding the Darkling—the most powerful of the Grisha—across the dangerous and terrifying Shadow Fold, Alina is unexpectedly revealed to have incredible powers and is packed off to train with the Grisha. There, she must determine who her friends and enemies are, even while falling under the spell of the charismatic Darkling.

Emilia di Carlo and her sister Vittoria are very different—Emilia is bookish and shy, Vittoria outgoing and brash—but they share a secret: They’re both streghe, and have spent their lives learning to use magic. In this version of Italy, the Malvagi (the seven princes of Hell) haven’t been seen in a long time, but a terrifying accident summons the Prince of Wrath and leaves three witches dead, including Vittoria. Emilia swears to use her power to avenge her sister, but when her revenge is delayed and she’s forced to work with Wrath, unwanted feelings begin to tick up the spice level to an uncomfortable degree.

#3383. ‘Bedford Park’ Trailer: Sundance Winner Stars Moon Choi, Who Falls for the Other Driver in Her Mother’s Car Accident

The last person Audrey (Moon Choi) wants to share a ride with is Eli (Son Sukku), the other driver in her mother’s car accident. But when the New York physical therapist returns to her childhood home in New Jersey to care for her suddenly injured parent (Won Mi Kyung), Audrey finds herself carpooling with the local security guard — now without a car of his own.

Hannah covers horror, sci-fi, and games at Collider, where she writes news and features, reviews new releases, and interviews the people who make them. She’s helping build out Collider’s gaming coverage, with Pokémon as one of her specialties. If she isn’t writing about a monster, she’s probably watching one on a tape from her VHS collection.

There’s something very funny about being able to vote for Grand Theft Auto 6 for Game of the Year before being able to play it. Apparently, spending years waiting for Rockstar’s next game wasn’t enough anticipation. Now players get to wonder whether it deserves the biggest award in gaming while they’re still waiting for their preorders to unlock. It could be a masterpiece. It could be a masterpiece, and based on the reviews, it might actually justify every bit of excitement surrounding it. Surely, then, a game that good could survive being considered at next year’s ceremony.

On November 17, GTA 6 received a Game of the Year nomination two days ahead of its November 19 release. It joins Control Resonant, Resident Evil Requiem, 007 First Light, Phantom Blade Zero, and The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time in the category. That’s a lineup that opens up plenty of opinions already, but Rockstar’s inclusion creates a question that has very little to do with whether the game is good: why are nominations being announced before all the eligible games are even widely available? The answer involves early access, voting deadlines, and an eligibility window that makes this perfectly acceptable, all of which explains how it happened without making it seem any less silly.

The Game Awards’ rules require games to be commercially available by November 20 at 9 p.m. PT, which puts GTA 6 inside the window by a single day. Publishers are also allowed to provide advance copies so voting outlets can evaluate games before submitting their ballots. There’s no special exception required here. The process already accommodates a game receiving a nomination while customers are still waiting to buy it. That's a distinction that's important to make, because the argument falls apart if it becomes an accusation that Rockstar somehow cheated. A publisher releasing an eligible game and providing access to critics is doing what the rules allow. The more frustrating part is that everyone can follow those rules and still end up here. An award intended to celebrate the year’s achievements has selected its contenders before the year it’s assessing has technically finished.

Advance review access makes sense. Games can take dozens of hours to finish, and readers deserve useful criticism when deciding whether to spend their money. Reviews have a reason to meet a release date, but A Game of the Year nomination doesn’t have that same responsibility. Nobody needs a trophy campaign underway to decide whether to pick up GTA 6, and Rockstar is hardly struggling to make people aware that it exists or excited to play the best-rated game in history. Putting it into the next awards cycle would give players time to experience what the jury is celebrating, and it would also give the game time to establish a reputation beyond the extraordinary excitement of finally being available. If that sounds like a disadvantage, it’s worth asking why an award for quality should depend so heavily on catching a game at its most exciting.

Four people, four completely different ways of being somebody's family. Here is your seat at the table, what the rest of them would rely on you for, and the thing you would have to watch.

You are the head of the table, and you did not ask for the job so much as end up holding it. Dom is the gravity of this franchise, which is why the films work best when everybody else is circling around whatever he has decided.

You are the one who says the thing out loud and then does not take it back. Letty is the least sentimental person at that table and somehow the most loyal, which is a combination almost nobody manages.

You are the reason anybody remembers the night. Roman talks first, thinks second and is far more frightened than he lets on, which is precisely what makes him the most human person in the whole family.

You are the one who made the plan work while everybody else was busy being heroic about it. Tej does not need the credit, which is fortunate, because in this family the credit tends to go to whoever drove fastest.

An early release has a long road to awards season. Players finish it, talk about the ending, replay their favorite sections, and start noticing the things that bothered them. The side quests that seemed endless in a good way might eventually feel endless in a much less flattering way. An opening that promised something extraordinary might turn out to be the best part. The opposite happens, too. A game can become more impressive with distance, when a story’s choices have had time to settle or another playthrough reveals how carefully everything was put together. Having months to think about a game can strengthen the case for it, it just doesn’t tend to generate the same noise as a massive new release finally arriving.

A November game enters that conversation under very different circumstances. People are still discovering its surprises and sending their friends messages about whatever ridiculous thing just happened. That excitement is part of what makes games wonderful, but it also makes comparison difficult. One contender is being judged against the memory of an experience while another is still delivering it.

GTA 6 takes that imbalance a step further because its nomination was announced before the public could begin having the experience at all. Whatever the voting outlets had played, most of the audience was still working from trailers, previews, and expectations. The nomination became another reason to get excited about the launch, alongside everything Rockstar had already done to sell it. None of that proves an earlier release deserves to win instead. Resident Evil Requiem obviously doesn’t become the better game between the two just because it has been around longer, and GTA 6 doesn’t become worse because it arrived later in the year. But the ceremony should be interested in giving those games a fair comparison, especially when the calendar is something it can actually control.

The actual problem here is actually pretty easy to address: close the eligibility window before nomination ballots are due. Let every qualifying game reach players before the contenders are announced. Games released afterward can compete the following year, when their developers’ work will still exist and their best moments will still be worth celebrating. That won’t make every nomination universally beloved. Nothing could. This is the gaming industry, after all, and nothing will ever be universally beloved, even GTA 6. It won’t erase recency bias, either, but it would stop the ceremony from asking its audience to vote on a field that wasn’t fully available when it was selected. That seems like a fairly reasonable expectation for an event built around celebrating games people love.

Rockstar may have made something extraordinary, and its developers could deserve every award coming their way. But a game this good shouldn’t need to squeeze into an eligibility window before players can even get their hands on it. If GTA 6 is the achievement its reviews suggest, its case would still hold up next year. The biggest award in gaming should go to the game that stays with people even after they've finished it, and anything worthy of that honor can surely survive the wait until next year.

#3379. All 13 Episodes Of This Masterpiece Detective Series Are Perfect From Start To Finish

One of the best detective series of all time has no bad episodes, with all of its seasons being perfect from start to finish, and it focuses on a character viewers know well. With the growth of streaming services, mystery shows and thrillers have become quite popular. After all, they pair off well with the concept of binge-watching, which is a streaming hit.

In 2026 alone, some of the best TV shows were mystery-filled series. On Prime Video, Young Sherlock and Sterling Point fit that bill, with the first being more fun, while the second was more dramatic. Netflix's His & Hers and I Will Find You were both crime thrillers with key mysteries at the center of their narratives, and they broke into the streamer's all-time TV show rankings.

As far as full-on detective TV shows go, there are also plenty of different concepts to choose from. The rise of murder mysteries since Rian Johnson's Knives Out conquered the box office has led to shows like Poker Face, DTF St. Louis, The Residence, Only Murders in the Building, and more. That said, we all know who is the most famous detective in fiction.

That would be Sherlock Holmes, an icon who has endured the test of time. There have been several Sherlock Holmes adaptations over the years, including movies, TV shows, video games, audio dramas, and more. That said, perhaps the best of them was BBC's Sherlock, starring Benedict Cumberbatch as the detective, with Martin Freeman co-starring as his loyal friend, John Watson. Sherlock has no bad episodes.

Sherlock debuted in 2010, with 13 episodes being released between then and 2017. It has been nearly a decade since the show last aired a new episode, which is disappointing, given how Cumberbatch and Freeman perfectly embodied their characters. As a modern Sherlock Holmes tale, the detective series made the lead character a quick-thinker who used all available technology to solve mysteries and worked as a detective consultant alongside Watson, DI Greg Lestrade, and more. Rather than being canceled, like most shows are in this streaming age, Sherlock stopped releasing new episodes due to its actors' busy schedules.

As it stands, Sherlock consists of four seasons with 12 episodes and a special. All of them clock in at around 90 minutes, feeling like movies in their own right, though with overall connective tissue including character arcs, dynamics, and so on. On IMDB, the lowest-rated episode of the detective series is season 4's "The Six Thatchers," which still comes in at a high 7.6 user score. On the other end, season 2's "The Reichenbach Fall" goes all the way up to masterpiece status with a series high 9.6 score. That episode culminated the story of Andrew Scott's James Moriarty.

While there are effectively no bad episodes of the BBC's Sherlock series, that is not to say that the show did not deal with its fair share of controversies over the years. How the show handled the end of Moriarty's storyline in the season 2 finale and the absence of the character who was the perfect foil to Cumberbatch's Sherlock did impact overall enjoyment of the series. That is also when the show's direction changed from more traditional clever mysteries to a psychological thriller.

Sherlock also poked fun at the fan theories surrounding the fallout of "The Reichenbach Fall," which was not seen as a positive. That said, perhaps the detective series' most controversial decision might have been its final, as the last episode of Sherlock was centered on Holmes' lost sister, Eurus, and made her nearly superhuman, as her high intellect allowed Eurus to essentially mind-control people just by talking to them, which is where many believe Sherlock jumped the shark. So, even though Sherlock has no bad episodes, its more controversial decisions have led to its overall reputation not being pristine.

As this in-depth explainer from Adaptive Security describes, most emails are encrypted in transit via Transport Layer Security (TLS), which prevents anyone from reading your message as it travels from server to server. However, encryption is temporarily stripped at each server: content is received and processed in plaintext and then re-encrypted when it leaves, meaning it could be read, logged, and distributed by the server provider.

Emails are also typically encrypted at rest—for example, while sitting on Google's servers and in a Gmail recipient's inbox. But this only prevents someone with physical access to the server hardware from reading messages, as Google still holds the encryption key and can access stored data. And, as PCMag points out, Google is scanning your messages to a degree, and it (along with other email providers) can and will hand emails over to law enforcement and government agencies in some cases.

If you have an account with a major email provider like Gmail, Outlook, or Apple Mail, you can add a third-party tool that layers an encryption protocol like OpenPGP on top of your existing account. PCMag recommends PreVeil, SecureMyEmail, and Virtru (which is limited to Gmail users in Chrome) for those who want to keep their current emails. Mailvelope is a browser add-on (and therefore a desktop-only tool) available in Chrome, Firefox, and Edge, though it can also be installed on other browsers, like Brave, that are built on the same architecture. FlowCrypt integrates with Gmail and Google Workspace on desktop and mobile.

Note that enterprise users of Google Workspace and Microsoft 365 have access to true end-to-end encryption without third-party add-ons. Gmail's Confidential mode and Outlook's Encrypt feature, available to all users, are not E2EE equivalents, as Google and Microsoft, respectively, still manage the keys.

For those who are willing to start fresh with a new email address (or who have a custom domain), providers like Proton Mail or Tuta offer native end-to-end encryption. The caveat: by default, this is only between users on the same service, so from one Proton user to another. If you want to send an end-to-end encrypted email from Proton to a Gmail user, for example, you have to set up password protection (and share the password via another secure channel) or use a PGP-compatible tool like those listed above. You can also Proton's Gmail integration does allow for end-to-end encryption, but only if both Gmail parties are using the Proton integration.
